records.title: Impact of continuous glucose monitoring on patient-reported outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes: a Systematic Review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Impact of continuous glucose monitoring on patient-reported outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes: a Systematic Review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Introduction

This research intended to systematically evaluate the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) on the emotional well-being of individuals with type 2 diabetes. It focused on the effects of CGM in four distinct patient-reported outcome domains: diabetes distress (measured by the diabetes distress scale [DDS]), treatment satisfaction (diabetes treatment satisfaction questionnaire [DTSQ]), psychological well-being (world health organization-5 well-being index [WHO-5]), and health-related quality of life (EuroQol five-dimensional questionnaire [EQ-5D]).

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library were retrieved from inception until April 2026 to collect randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing CGM with self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG). After two researchers independently performed literature screening, data extraction, and quality assessment, meta-analysis was conducted using Stata 16.0.

Results

A total of 9 RCTs comprising 1,453 individuals were included. All five studies reporting treatment satisfaction (DTSQ) showed a direction of effect favoring CGM over SMBG, although the magnitude of improvement varied widely and heterogeneity was extremely high (I²=98.9%), precluding a meaningful single summary estimate. However, no statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of diabetes distress (DDS) [standardized mean difference (SMD)=-0.25, 95% confidence interval (CI) (-0.98, 0.17)], psychological well-being (WHO-5) [SMD = 0.08, 95% CI (-0.09, 0.25)], or health-related quality of life (EQ-5D) [SMD = 0.22, 95% CI (-0.20, 0.64)].

Conclusion

Current evidence indicates that CGM may improve treatment satisfaction in individuals with type 2 diabetes, although this finding is limited by very high heterogeneity. Its effects on alleviating diabetes distress, improving psychological well-being, and enhancing health-related quality of life remain unclear and should be further investigated.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD42025634725.

records.title: Digital pathology, image analysis, and artificial intelligence in liver disease.

content.title: Digital pathology, image analysis, and artificial intelligence in liver disease.
content.abstract: Advances in digital pathology, image analysis, and artificial intelligence (AI) are rapidly transforming how pathologists and researchers interact with tissue samples and enable the development of diagnostic tools that harness high-resolution whole-slide images; these advances are in turn creating new opportunities for research, education, and routine clinical care globally. Liver disease is no exception, and digital pathology and AI have many applications in the diagnosis of liver cancer and liver diseases and in the assessment and management of transplantation. Although quantitative image analysis techniques have been applied to liver disease in research settings for over 50 years, recent improvements in image resolution, data storage, and the availability of advanced AI methods such as deep learning have driven multiple exciting developments. In this Review, we summarise the advancements in digital pathology, image analysis, and AI in liver disease. Key challenges such as access to and the logistics of using digital solutions, quality issues, and appropriate guidance in research and clinical use are reviewed, along with potential solutions to these challenges in the context of liver pathology and liver disease. Digital technologies are well established in liver pathology research, and access in clinical practice is increasing, with potential to address current laboratory challenges. Further evaluation is required to assess real-world effectiveness, clinical safety, and implementation of AI tools in liver pathology.

records.title: Diagnostic accuracy of traditional and deep learning methods for detecting depression based on speech features: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Diagnostic accuracy of traditional and deep learning methods for detecting depression based on speech features: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Depression diagnosis faces challenges of subjectivity and delay. Speech features offer potential objective biomarkers, but a systematic comparison of traditional machine learning (TML) and deep learning (DL) models is lacking.

Objective

To evaluate and compare the diagnostic accuracy of TML and DL models for depression detection using speech features, and to examine subgroup effects across sample size, validation strategy, language, and diagnostic criteria.

Methods

Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched 9 databases (PubMed, Medline, Embase, PsycINFO, Scopus, IEEE, Cochrane, ACM Digital Library, and Web of Science) from inception to April 2025. Eligible studies included clinically diagnosed patients with depression and healthy controls, assessed using speech-based TML or DL models, and reporting sensitivity, specificity, or the area under the curve (AUC). Risk of bias was evaluated using the diagnostic Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2). Random-effects bivariate models pooled diagnostic performance, and heterogeneity, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses were conducted.

Results

Twenty-five studies met the inclusion criteria (9 TML, 16 DL). TML models showed pooled sensitivity of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.74-0.88), specificity 0.83 (95% CI: 0.75-0.90), and AUC 0.89 (95% CI: 0.86-0.92). DL models achieved pooled sensitivity of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77-0.88), specificity 0.86 (95% CI: 0.80-0.90), and AUC 0.91 (95% CI: 0.89-0.93). Subgroup analyses indicated that diagnostic performance varied by sample size, validation strategy, language, and diagnostic criteria.

Conclusion

Both TML and DL models demonstrate good diagnostic accuracy in speech-based depression detection. ​The marginal but consistent superiority of DL models supports their potential use in secondary care settings for confirmatory diagnosis, while TML remains valuable for primary care screening.​​.

Clinical trial number

Not applicable.

records.title: The Parallel Consultation: A Literature Review of Patient Use of Large Language Models and Its Implications for Psychiatric Clinical Decision-Making.

content.title: The Parallel Consultation: A Literature Review of Patient Use of Large Language Models and Its Implications for Psychiatric Clinical Decision-Making.
content.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are immensely popular, being adopted by the general public for information and assistance in tasks, and increasingly in mental health support. This is especially true at a time when psychiatric care is limited by cost, availability, and stigma. More patients are using generative artificial intelligence (AI) for mental health guidance without professional medical oversight, and without disclosing usage to practitioners. This creates a clinical blind spot in which there lies a gap between what the practitioner knows and what has already altered the patient's presentation. Undisclosed AI use can undermine the trust-building cycle in a clinical relationship, as patients may defer trust to a source the clinician is not aware exists, while arriving with AI-generated interpretations that might differ from clinical judgment. This narrative literature review synthesizes emerging evidence of how patient use of LLMs can complicate psychiatric clinical decision-making to raise awareness among mental health practitioners. Patients report utilizing AI to augment or substitute for therapy due to cost and accessibility, and finding the experience to be validating and non-judgmental. Having received potentially biased or inaccurate AI-generated information, patients may present with AI-generated self-diagnoses, altering symptom framing and affecting treatment adherence and the therapeutic relationship. Daily interactions with AI chatbots have been reported to coincide with delusional thinking, contributing to an emerging phenomenon of AI-associated psychosis, putting patients further at risk. The variation in the types of AI chatbots also raises safety concerns, including hallucination, sycophancy, and model bias. These risks dramatically change how a patient may present themselves in a clinical encounter. To screen for AI use at intake as well as practitioner education to recognize sycophancy and other AI-associated risks, frameworks developed by professional societies are all needed. Prospective research designs to study the tools patients use are lacking. The clinical reality is that patients and technology are both outpacing the clinical training and guidelines needed to address this growing challenge.

records.title: Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence-Based Nursing Interventions for Chronic Illness Care: Umbrella Review.

content.title: Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence-Based Nursing Interventions for Chronic Illness Care: Umbrella Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI)-based nursing interventions are increasingly being used to manage chronic illnesses; however, their definitive impact on clinical outcomes remains inconclusive, necessitating a comprehensive evidence synthesis.

Objective

This umbrella review aimed to synthesize the evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI-based nursing interventions for chronic illness care and their subsequent impact on health care outcomes in clinical settings.

Methods

We conducted an umbrella review and prospectively registered the protocol. A systematic search of 5 electronic databases (PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science) was performed to identify systematic reviews and meta-analyses published in English between 2021 and 2025. The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist.

Results

Eight high-quality systematic reviews were included, with machine learning identified as the predominant technology. Three primary outcome domains emerged: predictive, psychosocial, and hospital utilization. Due to measurement heterogeneity, the results were synthesized narratively. Our findings demonstrated that AI-based nursing interventions are effective in predicting adverse clinical events, unplanned hospital utilization, and health care costs. However, evidence regarding psychosocial outcomes remains insufficient.

Conclusions

This review provides systematic evidence supporting the utility of AI in chronic illness management, particularly for improving predictive and utilization outcomes. These findings offer actionable insights for nursing leaders to integrate AI into clinical practice and education. Future research should prioritize rigorous empirical designs to further strengthen the evidence base for AI-driven nursing care.

records.title: Prognostic value of NLR, SII, PCT, and PLR in sepsis and septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Prognostic value of NLR, SII, PCT, and PLR in sepsis and septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Importance

Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host responses to infection. Accessible inflammatory biomarkers may improve early risk stratification for mortality or short-term adverse prognosis in septic patients.

Objective

To systematically evaluate the prognostic associations of four routinely available inflammatory biomarkers (NLR, PLR, PCT, SII) with mortality or short-term adverse prognosis in patients with sepsis and septic shock. Three PROSPERO protocol deviations (CRD420251035190) were documented: the research question, biomarker set, and effect-measure synthesis all changed from the registered protocol.

Methods

Ten cohort studies involving 2,412 patients were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed, with OR and HR analyzed separately, and continuous and categorical effects synthesized separately.

Results

Two studies reported PCT with endpoint-specific estimates (Wang 2024 mortality OR = 1.957 [1.243-3.081]; Li Liang 2024 composite OR = 2.827 [1.694-4.718]; not pooled per §2.5). SII showed a significant HR-based association [pooled HR = 1.4112 (1.2568-1.5846); P < 0.0001; I2 = 0.0%; k = 2]. Continuous NLR showed minimal heterogeneity in the primary OR-based synthesis [pooled OR = 1.0146 per unit (1.0098-1.0195); P < 0.001; I2 = 0.0%; k = 2; Ren 2022 + Song 2025]; the exploratory analysis including the Wang 2024-recalc value yielded OR = 0.9660 [0.9121-1.0230]; I2 = 96.3%; P = 0.237. PLR was not significant [pooled OR = 1.7491 (0.9597-3.1877); P = 0.0679; I2 = 95.4%].

Conclusion

The present meta-analysis does not support strong clinical recommendations. The evidence is hypothesis-generating and should be interpreted with caution due to three major PROSPERO protocol deviations, moderate-to-high risk of bias, small sample sizes for PCT and SII, and substantial heterogeneity for PLR and exploratory NLR. These biomarkers should be interpreted as components of multidimensional risk assessment, not stand-alone prognostic tools.

Systematic review registration

PROSPERO ID CRD420251035190.

records.title: Application of artificial intelligence in cervical cytology: a systematic review of deep learning models, datasets, and reported metrics.

content.title: Application of artificial intelligence in cervical cytology: a systematic review of deep learning models, datasets, and reported metrics.
content.abstract:
Introduction

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in cervical cytology has increased substantially due to the need for automated tools that support the early detection of precancerous lesions.

Methods

This systematic review examined deep learning models applied to cervical cytology images, focusing on the architectures used, the datasets employed, and the performance metrics reported. Articles published between 2022 and 2025 were retrieved from Scopus using PRISMA methodology. After applying inclusion criteria and full-text screening, 77 studies were included for RQ1 (models), 75 for RQ2 (datasets), and 71 for RQ3 (metrics).

Results

Hybrid models were the most prevalent (56%), followed by convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and a growing number of Vision Transformer (ViT)-based approaches. SIPaKMeD and Herlev were the most frequently used datasets, although the use of private datasets is increasing. Accuracy was the most commonly reported metric (mean 87.76%), followed by precision, recall, and F1-score. Several hybrid and ViT-based models exceeded 92% accuracy. Identified limitations included limited cross-validation, reduced clinical representativeness of datasets, and inconsistent diagnostic criteria.

Discussion

This review synthesizes current trends in AI-based cervical cytology, highlights common methodological limitations, and proposes directions for future research to enhance clinical applicability and standardization.

records.title: Machine learning-based diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder in children and adolescents using eye-tracking data: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Machine learning-based diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder in children and adolescents using eye-tracking data: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

Eye-tracking technology has been increasingly investigated as an objective approach for distinguishing individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) from typically developing (TD) individuals. Artificial intelligence and machine learning (ML) methods have been widely applied to support ASD diagnosis and treatment, and prior studies suggest that ML models leveraging eye-tracking data can achieve high diagnostic accuracy. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of machine-learning models using eye-tracking data to distinguish children and adolescents with ASD from TD peers.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from inception to August 3, 2025. We included studies that applied ML methods to eye-tracking data to distinguish children with ASD from TD children. We extracted data on participant characteristics, model performance, eye-tracking protocols, and machine-learning algorithms. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251162462).

Results

We identified 1,045 records, of which 25 studies were included in the meta-analysis. The included studies comprised 2,319 participants, with sample sizes ranging from 32 to 529 per study. The pooled accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of machine-learning models using eye-tracking data to distinguish children with ASD from TD children were 85 % (95 % CI, 81-89 %), 86 % (95 % CI, 82-89 %), and 86 % (95 % CI, 79-91 %), respectively. These results suggest that eye-tracking-based machine-learning approaches have good diagnostic performance for identifying ASD.

Conclusion

Eye-tracking-based machine-learning approaches show considerable potential for distinguishing children with ASD from TD children. However, the robustness and generalizability of these findings are limited by the lack of external validation, small sample sizes, and substantial between-study heterogeneity. To establish generalizability, future research should prioritize standardized eye-tracking paradigms and large-scale, prospective, multicenter study designs with external validation. Such efforts may facilitate the translation of these models into clinical practice as objective and efficient adjunctive screening tools.

records.title: Non-pharmacological therapy for pediatric adenoid hypertrophy: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.

content.title: Non-pharmacological therapy for pediatric adenoid hypertrophy: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Adenoid hypertrophy (AH) is a common chronic inflammatory condition in children and a major cause of upper airway obstruction. Although acupuncture- and moxibustion-based therapies have been used as adjunctive treatments for pediatric AH, the relative efficacy of different modalities remains uncertain. Therefore, this network meta-analysis was conducted to compare the efficacy of different acupuncture and moxibustion interventions for pediatric AH.

Methods

Eight databases were searched from their inception to May 1, 2025, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) related to acupuncture for AH. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB 2.0) tool. Network meta-analysis was conducted using R 4.2.0 and Stata 14.0 software.

Results

Seven kinds of acupuncture and moxibustion adjuvant intervention measures were studied, including conventional acupuncture (CA), electroacupuncture (EA), warm acupuncture (WA), conventional moxibustion (CM), thunder-fire moxibustion (TM), sandwiched moxibustion (SM), and acupoint application (AA). Adenoid/nasopharynx ratio (A/N), nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, and snore were analyzed. RoB2.0 results showed most studies were judged as having some concerns or high risk of bias, and sensitivity analysis showed low heterogeneity. CINeMA showed the confidence ratings of different treatment comparisons were judged as very low to low. The network meta-analysis demonstrated that CA + TCMs (traditional Chinese medicine) showed a clinically relevant improvement in the A/N ratio. CM + TCMs exhibited superior efficacy for nasal obstruction [MD = -1.22, 95%CI(-1.82, -0.62), P < 0.05] and mouth breathing [MD = -1.04, 95%CI(-1.43, -0.65), P < 0.05]. CA + EA + WA demonstrated advantage for snore reduction [MD = -1.00, 95%CI(-1.70, -0.30), P < 0.05].

Conclusion

Acupuncture- and moxibustion-based adjunctive therapies may be associated with improvements in symptoms and radiological outcomes in pediatric adenoid hypertrophy. However, the certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to low, and these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/home, identifier CRD420251052651.

records.title: Towards Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: A Review of Perturbation and Backpropagation-Based Methods.

content.title: Towards Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: A Review of Perturbation and Backpropagation-Based Methods.
content.abstract: Machine and deep learning algorithms have been proven their efficiency in the medical domain. This is particularly noticeable in medical imaging, where these algorithms have demonstrated exceptional capabilities, often surpassing human experts in detecting diseases, segmenting anatomical structures, and in aiding diagnosis. However, despite their high performance, the non-transparency of these models has raised concerns about trust and explainability, especially in critical domains, such as healthcare. Explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as a promising field that, aims to make the decision-making processes of AI systems more interpretable and understandable to humans. By offering clear, human-understandable justifications, XAI enhances clinicians' trust in AI-assisted decisions, and supports the safe integration of these technologies into clinical workflows. This paper focuses on perturbation-based and backpropagation-based explainability methods that are widely adopted for convolutional neural networks in medical imaging. We intend to provide deeper insight into the relevance of XAI methods in medical imaging. We propose a structured taxonomy that categorizes these methods into perturbation and backpropagation-based approaches. For each category, we highlight their respective strengths, limitations, and areas of applicability. Furthermore, we discuss the key challenges hindering the adoption of XAI and identify promising research directions to bridge the gap between high-performance AI models and their responsible deployment in real-world healthcare environments.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence for Assessing the Relationship Between Mandibular Third Molars and the Inferior Alveolar Nerve on Panoramic Radiographs: A Systematic Review.
records.publisher: Medicina oral, patologia oral y cirugia bucal

content.title: Artificial Intelligence for Assessing the Relationship Between Mandibular Third Molars and the Inferior Alveolar Nerve on Panoramic Radiographs: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Extracting mandibular third molars is a common procedure that carries a risk of injury to the inferior alveolar nerve (IAN). Panoramic radiographs (PR) are commonly used for preoperative assessment of the mandibular third molars, but they are not very reliable for evaluating the relationship of the IAN. This systematic review aims to evaluate the accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI) models in assessing the relationship between mandibular third molars and the IAN.

Materials and methods

We conducted systematic searches in MEDLINE (via PubMed), the Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus for studies published between January 2020 and April 2026. Eligible studies evaluated artificial intelligence systems that analyze panoramic radiographs to assess the relationship between mandibular third molars and the IAN, using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) or expert assessments as references. The studies had to report key diagnostic performance metrics. Two independent reviewers carried out study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessments using the QUADAS-2 tool.

Results

We included eleven studies with more than 9,700 patients. The AI models reviewed, including architectures such as ResNet, VGG, and YOLO, demonstrated promising diagnostic performance. Their accuracy ranged from 0.630 to 0.896, with sensitivity and specificity reaching up to 0.92 and 0.95, respectively. No single architecture was consistently superior, but AI models outperformed less experienced human observers in the studies that included this comparison. Validation against CBCT usually yielded more reliable performance metrics than validation based solely on expert opinion.

Conclusions

AI models show promise as decision-support tools in the radiographic assessment of the relationship between mandibular third molars and the inferior alveolar nerve on panoramic radiographs. However, variations in datasets, reference standards, and validation methods across studies mean that no single architecture can yet be considered superior. Larger, multicenter, prospective studies with external validation are necessary to confirm these systems' performance before they can be widely used in clinical practice.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation: A Narrative Review of Deep Learning Methods, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions.
records.publisher: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation: A Narrative Review of Deep Learning Methods, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions.
content.abstract: Ischemic stroke management is time-sensitive, and lesion segmentation supports treatment selection, prognostication, and reproducible quantification. Deep learning (DL) aims to accelerate and standardize lesion delineation to augment neuroimaging workflows. We conducted a narrative review of DL-based ischemic stroke lesion segmentation studies published from 2020 to 2025. PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched; ~ 500 records were identified, and 40 full-text studies were included after screening. We extracted imaging modality, architecture, segmentation targets, and reported performance (primarily Dice similarity coefficient [DSC]) for descriptive synthesis; exploratory LOESS curves were used only to visualize broader temporal trends and were not interpreted inferentially. U-Net backbones and variants remained dominant, with gains from residual and attention mechanisms and standardized pipelines. On MRI (especially DWI/ADC), many studies reported DSC > 0.80; residual/attention U-Nets reached ~ 0.87 and nnU-Net achieved ~ 0.80-0.82. Since 2023, transformer-based and ensemble approaches have increasingly appeared among top-performing MRI models, with multisite DWI reports approaching ~ 0.90. CT/NCCT segmentation was more variable, with typical research DSC ~ 0.35-0.65, but late-period hybrid CNN-transformer, ensemble, and multimodal approaches reported DSC approaching ~ 0.8, and NCCT tools report higher performance. Overall trends suggested gradual improvement for MRI and a U-shaped trajectory for CT. DL stroke lesion segmentation is maturing toward clinical viability, most convincingly for MRI, while CT applications remain constrained by subtle early ischemic change and generalization challenges. Many studies remain retrospective and may not reflect real-world performance and access constraints, reinforcing the need for prospective, multicenter validation and scalable deployment pathways to enable equitable impact.

records.title: Platelet-rich plasma for wound healing and scar formation after cesarean section: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Platelet-rich plasma for wound healing and scar formation after cesarean section: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Surgical wound complications follow 3-15% of cesarean deliveries globally. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP), an autologous concentrate of growth factors, has documented regenerative activity across several surgical disciplines, yet no quantitative synthesis of randomized trial evidence has been published for its intraoperative use during cesarean section.

Methods

PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, Scopus, and Web of Science were systematically searched from inception through March 2026 to identify randomized controlled trials comparing intraoperative PRP with standard care during cesarean section. Primary outcomes were skin scar quality measured with the Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS), the Vancouver Scar Scale (VSS), or the Manchester Scar Scale; early wound inflammation measured with the Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge, and Approximation (REEDA) scale; and uterine scar integrity defined by niche formation rate and residual myometrial thickness. Secondary outcomes were postoperative pain on visual analogue or numeric rating scales and analgesic consumption. Standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) were pooled using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model. Ambiguity regarding dispersion measures in one study was resolved through p-value back-calculation, and sensitivity analyses were pre-specified. The protocol was registered prospectively (INPLASY202640041; doi: https://doi.org/10.37766/inplasy2026.4.0041 ).

Results

Five randomized trials enrolling 366 women across five countries were included, with four trials (n = 336) contributing to skin-scar synthesis. PRP improved patient-reported scar quality (POSAS-patient SMD - 0.50, 95% CI - 0.83 to - 0.17; p = 0.003; I² = 0%) and clinician-assessed scar quality (POSAS-observer SMD - 0.42, 95% CI - 0.75 to - 0.10; p = 0.012; I² = 32%), and reduced early wound inflammation (REEDA SMD - 0.52, 95% CI - 0.84 to - 0.20; p = 0.002; I² = 0%; sensitivity analysis under the naive SD assumption produced I² = 98% and was uninterpretable). In a single small trial that targeted the uterine scar, PRP reduced niche formation from 46.7% to 13.3% (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.07-1.16; Fisher's exact p = 0.109 on the binary 2 × 2 table). Vancouver Scar Scale heterogeneity precluded pooling (I² = 94%). Visual analogue pain at early time points was not significantly reduced (pooled SMD - 0.22, 95% CI - 0.50 to + 0.06; p = 0.12). No safety event attributable to PRP was reported in any trial.

Conclusions

Across a small and clinically heterogeneous evidence base of five randomized trials, intraoperative PRP improves cesarean skin scar quality and reduces early wound inflammation, while early pain intensity does not appear to be affected. The single trial that addressed the uterine scar suggests a substantial reduction in niche formation, but with only thirty patients, an unreproducible study-reported p-value, and a Fisher's exact p of 0.109 on the binary outcome, this signal is hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in adequately powered trials before any change in practice can be considered.

Protocol registration

INPLASY202640041 (doi: https://doi.org/10.37766/inplasy2026.4.0041 ).

records.title: Efficacy of Epimedii Folium and related preparations in experimental osteoporosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Efficacy of Epimedii Folium and related preparations in experimental osteoporosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Epimedii Folium and related extracts have shown osteogenic, antiresorptive, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory activities in experimental studies. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated their efficacy in rodent models of osteoporosis.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang Data were searched from their inception to 13 June 2026. Controlled in vivo studies using rat or mouse models of osteoporosis or experimentally induced bone loss were eligible. Random-effects models generated Hedges' standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE tool. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261428223). Sensitivity analyses examined heterogeneity, the influence of the Qi 2019 estimate, and the effects of multi-arm dependence, preparation type, disease model, duration, and dose. Certainty was appraised using an adaptation of GRADE for preclinical animal evidence.

Results

Twenty-nine independent rodent studies were included. Femoral BMD increased (20 comparisons from 9 studies; SMD = 1.66, 95% CI: 1.07-2.25; 95% prediction interval [PI]: -0.61 to 3.93; I2 = 73.77%). Excluding Qi 2019 reduced the SMD to 1.44 (95% CI: 0.96-1.92), while a three-level study-cluster robust model yielded an SMD of 2.25 (95% CI: 0.40-4.10). The average effects favored several regional BMD, microarchitectural, and biomechanical outcomes, but the majority of PIs crossed the null. PINP was not significant. The Systematic Review Centre for Laboratory Animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) assessment found that the majority of judgments were unclear, with nine domain-level judgments rated as high risk; certainty was very low.

Conclusion

Random-effects pooled estimates favored the examined oral Epimedii Folium-derived preparations for several regional BMD, trabecular microarchitecture, and ex vivo biomechanical outcomes in rodent models. However, wide prediction intervals, chemical and model heterogeneity, small study sizes, incomplete reporting, and correlated multi-arm comparisons limit confidence in the pooled effect magnitudes. Chemically standardized preparations and exposure-informed dosing are needed before clinical translation.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261428223, identifier CRD420261428223.

records.title: Depression comorbidity in children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Depression comorbidity in children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Depression is a frequent psychological comorbidity among youth with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), yet reported prevalence rates vary widely across studies. This meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of depression and explore sources of heterogeneity.

Methods

This meta-analysis is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251126166). We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and PsycINFO from inception to October 24, 2025. The pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression were conducted to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity. All processes of study screening, data extraction, and quality assessment were carried out independently by two researchers.

Results

Seventeen studies comprising 5,215 participants were included. The pooled prevalence of comorbid depression was 23.1% (95% CI: 18.0%-29.1%), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 93%). Subgroup analyses indicated that prevalence differed significantly by HbA1c level and assessment method. Participants with HbA1c < 7% showed higher prevalence (52.0%) than those with HbA1c ≥ 7% (24.0%). Studies using self-report scales reported higher prevalence (25.2%) than those using clinical diagnostic criteria (12.2%). Univariate meta-regression indicated that both HbA1c level and the depression assessment method significantly influenced the reported prevalence of depression.

Conclusions

Approximately one in four youth with T2DM experience depression. Variations in assessment method and glycemic control may contribute to the heterogeneity of reported prevalence. These findings underscore the importance of standardized diagnostic procedures and early psychological screening in pediatric T2DM populations to improve both mental health and diabetes outcomes.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420251126166.

records.title: Towards Acoustic Bioindicator Integration in AI-Based Wildfire Monitoring: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Towards Acoustic Bioindicator Integration in AI-Based Wildfire Monitoring: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract: Wildfires are becoming more frequent, severe, and long-lasting, driving rapid growth in sensor-based and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled systems for early detection and risk assessment. This article presents a systematic literature review, based on 169 studies screened from 7511 records, of wildfire monitoring approaches using satellite and aerial remote sensing, fixed cameras, wireless sensor networks, and Internet of Things (IoT) platforms combined with machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models for ignition detection, fire-weather indices, spread prediction, and burned-area mapping. The review organizes existing work by sensing modality, spatial and temporal scale, learning task, model type, and deployment architecture, and identifies the environmental drivers most commonly used across systems, including temperature, humidity, vegetation state, drought indices, and smoke or air quality. Based on this analysis, the review summarizes key technical challenges, including data sparsity in remote regions, high false-alarm rates, limited edge resources, and difficulty fusing heterogeneous data streams in real time. As an exploratory future direction, the review discusses bioindicator signals from wildlife and managed species, using honeybee colonies as a case example. Current bee bioacoustic studies support the detection of colony states and environmental stress proxies, but they do not yet validate wildfire or smoke detection. Therefore, this review proposes bee bioacoustics only as a potential complementary contextual signal for future hybrid wildfire monitoring systems.

records.title: The diagnostic value of radiomics-based machine learning for lymph node metastasis in prostate cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: The diagnostic value of radiomics-based machine learning for lymph node metastasis in prostate cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

The precise and noninvasive diagnosis of preoperative lymph node metastasis (LNM) in prostate cancer (PC) is challenging. Some studies have studied the application of radiomics-based machine learning (ML) for detecting LNM in PC. However, systematic evidence regarding its diagnostic performance is still lacking.

Aim

Our study aimed to systematically evaluate the accuracy of radiomics-based ML models in diagnosing LNM in PC, offering evidence-based support for the use of ML in clinical decision-making.

Methods

Cochrane, PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science were searched for eligible studies on the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML for LNM in PC until June 11, 2025. The risk of bias in the included studies was evaluated via the Radiomics Quality Score (RQS). Meta-analysis of sensitivity (SEN) and specificity (SPC) was performed using a bivariate mixed-effects model. Subgroup analyses were performed in the meta-analysis based on imaging modality and modeling approach. We conducted meta-analysis on the training and validation sets, respectively.

Results

A total of 22 studies were included, comprising 13 studies on positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT)-based radiomics and nine studies on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based radiomics. In the validation sets, models based on PET/CT yielded a pooled SEN of 0.89 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.75-0.96), SPC of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.63-0.93), and a summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) of 0.93 (95% CI: 0.77-0.98). Models based on MRI had a SEN of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.78-0.89), SPC of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.71-0.94), and a SROC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.71-0.97). Radiomics-based ML models yielded a SEN of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.76-0.91), a SPC of 0.77 (95% CI: 0.66-0.86), and an area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.72-0.96). In contrast, deep learning (DL) models based on radiomics demonstrated a higher SEN of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.75-0.95), SPC of 0.97 (95% CI: 0.58-1.00), and a SROC of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.19-1.00).

Conclusions

Radiomics demonstrates promising diagnostic performance in detecting LNM in PC. DL models show superior accuracy. Nevertheless, given the limited sample sizes, insufficient external validation, and heterogeneity in imaging protocols, future research should incorporate more multi-center images from different regions. Meanwhile, it is necessary to develop standardized imaging and segmentation protocols to improve transparency and reduce heterogeneity, thereby building more widely applicable and high-performance radiomics-based machine learning models to improve the performance of early detection of LNM in PC patients.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier PROSPERO CRD420251085724.

records.title: From monitoring to intervention: a closed-loop digital health framework for gaming disorder.

content.title: From monitoring to intervention: a closed-loop digital health framework for gaming disorder.
content.abstract: Gaming disorder has become a significant public health concern and represents a complex, dynamic condition that requires continuous risk monitoring throughout its progression. However, conventional assessment methods, which rely primarily on questionnaires and clinical interviews, are inherently static and retrospective, limiting dynamic monitoring and early risk identification. Although digital phenotyping, artificial intelligence (AI), and digital therapeutics have emerged as promising approaches, existing reviews have largely examined these technologies separately, lacking an integrated framework for intelligent gaming disorder management. This review systematically synthesizes current evidence on digital phenotyping, AI-driven risk prediction, and digital intervention strategies, and integrates them into a "Monitor-Predict-Intervene" closed-loop digital health framework. This study indicates that digital phenotyping enables continuous multimodal monitoring of behavioral, physiological, psychological, and social signals; AI facilitates dynamic risk stratification and trajectory prediction through multimodal data integration; and digital therapeutics, particularly Just-in-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs), deliver personalized interventions based on evolving risk states. Collectively, these technologies establish a closed-loop digital health paradigm that supports continuous risk management across the progression of gaming disorder. Overall, this framework advances gaming disorder management from static assessment to continuous monitoring, from reactive treatment to proactive prevention, and from standardized intervention to individualized precision care, while providing a conceptual foundation and translational roadmap for future digital mental health research and clinical practice. Future research should further address challenges related to data privacy, algorithm interpretability, and clinical implementation to facilitate the development of scalable and intelligent digital health systems.

records.title: Operationalising digital and AI pathology in translational research and drug development: an infrastructure and regulatory perspective from biobank to companion diagnostic.

content.title: Operationalising digital and AI pathology in translational research and drug development: an infrastructure and regulatory perspective from biobank to companion diagnostic.
content.abstract: Digital and artificial intelligence (AI) pathology have advanced rapidly and are increasingly embedded in translational research, clinical trials and regulated diagnostic devices. Multiple reviews have addressed the underlying computational methods, oncology applications and clinical translation barriers; however, the operational and regulatory infrastructure required to deploy these technologies across the full drug-development pipeline remains under-reviewed. This structured narrative review synthesises peer-reviewed literature and regulatory documents identified through searches of PubMed, Embase and Web of Science between January 2019 and April 2026 (78 sources retained) on the end-to-end ecosystem connecting AI-ready tissue biobanks, preclinical pathology, AI-assisted patient screening, clinical-trial endpoint adjudication, central pathology review, Contract Research Organization (CRO) workflows and US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulatory pathways governing In Vitro Diagnostics (IVD), Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and Companion Diagnostics (CDx). Unlike prior method-centric or oncology-clinician-centric reviews, we focus on the infrastructure between models and patients, including Laboratory Information Systems (LIS), Image Management Systems (IMS), AI orchestration and structured reporting under Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments, College of American Pathologists, Good Laboratory Practice, Good Clinical Laboratory Practice, Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act and FDA frameworks. We provide a vendor-agnostic comparison of integrated pathology platforms, a mapping of FDA regulatory pathways (510(k), De Novo, premarket approval) to digital-pathology product categories, a stage-by-stage map from each drug-development challenge to its enabling infrastructure and regulatory framework, and a critical appraisal of the unresolved bottlenecks that gate broad adoption: domain shift, interpretability, annotation cost, algorithmic bias, external validation, regulatory uncertainty and reimbursement. A governed, interoperable LIS, IMS and AI ecosystem is a prerequisite for translating digital-pathology research into regulator-grade evidence. Priorities include external validation against reporting standards (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis - Artificial Intelligence (TRIPOD-AI), Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM), Development and Early-stage Clinical Identification and Delegation Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (DECIDE-AI)), harmonisation with the EU AI Act and EU Medical Device Regulation and cost-effectiveness evaluation in real-world deployment.

records.title: Human Perceptions Compared to Large Language Models on the Future of Artificial Intelligence: A Phenomenological Comparative Study

content.title: Human Perceptions Compared to Large Language Models on the Future of Artificial Intelligence: A Phenomenological Comparative Study
content.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is currently undergoing exponential development that operates beyond traditional CPU transistor benchmarks like Moore's Law, propelled instead by domain-specific architectural scaling (Huang's Law) and massive cluster aggregation. This research investigates the divergence and convergence between Large Language Model (LLM) projections and human perceptions regarding a post-singularity future. Utilizing a hybrid phenomenological qualitative and quantitative methodology, we interviewed five major LLMs—Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet, OpenAI GPT-4o, Google Gemini 2.0 Flash, Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4), and xAI Grok 3—alongside a purposive sample of ten human participants. We introduced a persona-steering protocol to evaluate model output sensitivity when default corporate Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) politeness framing is stripped away, disclosing a pronounced shift towards more aggressive, urgent, and fatalistic narrative clusters. Findings show that while independent qualitative responses from humans and LLMs exhibited limited vocabulary overlap, participants displayed high agreement when subsequently evaluated against collated LLM future scenarios. This indicates a considerable "control risk", pointing to possible vulnerabilities concerning disinformation, liability, and the decline of human cognitive sovereignty. By documenting attitudes during the 2024–2025 acceleration period, this investigation identifies structural friction between technical AI capability expansion and public risk perception, offering an empirical foundation for future studies on cognitive sovereignty and human-AI alignment.

records.title: Legal and Regulatory Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Use in Medical and Radiology Research.
records.publisher: The Indian journal of radiology & imaging

content.title: Legal and Regulatory Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Use in Medical and Radiology Research.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical imaging and radiology research, improving image acquisition, interpretation, workflow efficiency, and decision support. However, its rapid adoption has introduced complex legal and regulatory challenges involving patient privacy, data governance, algorithm validation, liability, intellectual property, transparency, cybersecurity, and ethical oversight. A comprehensive understanding of the evolving legal landscape is essential for the safe, effective, and legally compliant implementation of AI in radiology.

Methods

A narrative review of the published literature and current regulatory guidance was conducted. Relevant international legal and regulatory frameworks governing AI in medical imaging were evaluated, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, General Data Protection Regulation, U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, World Health Organization recommendations, International Medical Device Regulators Forum principles, and selected national regulations. Key topics reviewed included data protection, informed consent, AI validation, regulatory approval pathways, post-market surveillance, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, explainability, and medico-legal responsibility.

Results

Current regulatory frameworks increasingly classify AI-enabled radiology software as SaMD, requiring risk-based evaluation, clinical validation, quality management systems, and continuous post-market performance monitoring. Regulatory authorities emphasize transparency, human oversight, data security, and lifecycle governance of AI systems. Nevertheless, important legal challenges remain, including liability for AI-assisted diagnostic errors, ownership of AI-generated outputs, secondary use of imaging data, cross-border data sharing, algorithmic bias, and regulation of adaptive or continuously learning AI models.

Conclusions

The legal framework governing AI in radiology is evolving in parallel with technological innovation. Responsible integration of AI into clinical practice and research requires harmonized international regulations, robust data governance, standardized validation protocols, transparent algorithm development, and clearly defined legal accountability. Continued collaboration among radiologists, researchers, regulators, policymakers, industry, and legal experts will be essential to ensure that AI technologies remain safe, ethical, equitable, and trustworthy while maximizing their potential to improve patient care.

records.title: A Case-Based Framework for Teaching Artificial Intelligence Applications in Medical Education.
records.publisher: MedEdPORTAL : the journal of teaching and learning resources

content.title: A Case-Based Framework for Teaching Artificial Intelligence Applications in Medical Education.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-based tools are emerging across many areas of medicine. The next generation of medical professionals must be prepared to critically assess the tools they will use, including how they work and the ethical or legal implications of their implementation. To address this need, we developed a generalizable case-writing framework that enables educators and learners to engage with clinical cases integrating AI/ML concepts, clinical reasoning, and ethical considerations.

Methods

We designed a case-writing template to compose clinical case scenarios that integrate clinical, technical, and ethical/legal learning objectives relating to AI applications in medicine. Medical students used this template to construct 3 cases. Student-authored cases were presented to a broader audience in 1-hour sessions: first as a pilot event, then as a class-wide lecture for 140 fourth-year medical students in a transition-into-residency course.

Results

After the sessions, student audiences had a statistically significant increase in familiarity with key AI terminology, a greater appreciation for the importance of ethical considerations of AI applications in health care, and an increased perceived importance of integrating AI-related topics into the medical curriculum.

Discussion

A case-based framework provides a scalable approach to integrating AI education into existing curricula by connecting clinical scenarios with technical concepts and the ethical considerations of AI adoption; cases offer a familiar format that helps learners understand AI applications in patient care while exploring implementation challenges. The case-writing template and 3 sample cases are provided as adaptable resources for educators seeking to incorporate AI literacy.

records.title: Integrating predictive modeling, imaging, and EHR-linked decision support in spine informatics.
records.publisher: European spine journal : official publication of the European Spine Society, the European Spinal Deformity Society, and the European Section of the Cervical Spine Research Society

content.title: Integrating predictive modeling, imaging, and EHR-linked decision support in spine informatics.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming spine care by enabling analysis of imaging, clinical, and textual data to support diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment planning. Techniques including deep learning-based image analysis, radiomics, and natural language processing (NLP) offer opportunities to standardize interpretation and derive quantitative biomarkers beyond human visual assessment. This narrative review examines recent innovations in spine-focused biomedical informatics and evaluates their clinical relevance and translational challenges.

Methods

A narrative review was conducted, focusing on AI in spine care across imaging, radiomics, NLP of electronic health records, and clinical decision support. Literature was selected via targeted PubMed searches; studies describing technical development, validation, and clinical implementation were synthesized, addressing explainability, uncertainty, workflow, and regulation.

Results

Convolutional neural networks enable vertebral and disc segmentation, detection of degenerative and traumatic pathology, and quantitative assessment of paraspinal musculature. Radiomics approaches extract high-dimensional imaging features that improve the prediction of osteoporosis, fracture risk, tumor characterization, and surgical outcomes. NLP techniques, including emerging large language models, unlock clinically relevant information from unstructured text, enhancing outcome prediction and population-level analyses. Multimodal clinical decision support systems integrating imaging, EHR data, and NLP-derived features demonstrate promise for personalized risk assessment and treatment guidance. Challenges remain regarding data heterogeneity, generalizability, privacy, and prospective validation.

Conclusion

AI-driven biomedical informatics holds substantial promise to enhance diagnostic accuracy, prognostication, and personalized decision-making in spine care. Successful clinical translation will require robust validation, explainable, uncertainty-aware models, regulatory alignment, and integration into clinical workflows to ensure safe, trustworthy, and patient-centered adoption.

records.title: Toward explainable traffic crash liability analysis via neural-symbolic multimodal reasoning: Integrating visual perception with legal knowledge graphs.

content.title: Toward explainable traffic crash liability analysis via neural-symbolic multimodal reasoning: Integrating visual perception with legal knowledge graphs.
content.abstract: Determining traffic crash liability relies on rigorous on-site evidence and legal provisions and involves substantial manual intervention and potential human error. However, intelligent traffic monitoring systems focus on detection and tracking and cannot provide structured, rule-grounded decision support for formal crash-liability analysis. Moreover, emerging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) suffer from object hallucination that distorts or omits physical evidence, and their opaque reasoning cannot produce explicit evidence-to-rule chains required for traceable and reviewable liability analysis. This paper proposes CrashLex, an explainable neural-symbolic decision-support framework that integrates visual perception with legal knowledge graph reasoning to align multimodal inference with predefined statutory rules and traceability requirements. Within CrashLex, a dual-query vision-language architecture employs parallel semantic and symbolic streams to mitigate object hallucination, utilizing Scene Queries for global context modeling and Perception Queries for fine-grained atomic feature extraction, respectively. The domain-specific legal knowledge graph maps these atomic facts from observable physical conditions to corresponding statutory elements, providing a structured basis for rule-grounded assessment. A logic-driven aggregation protocol then imposes explicit constraints derived from extracted facts and statutory provisions onto the inference process, thereby enabling traceable and interpretable preliminary liability assessment. On the held-out DeepAccident benchmark, CrashLex achieves a Legal Accuracy of 94.0% under the fixed legal-output evaluation protocol and an Object Hallucination Rate of 2.8%, corresponding to an 82.1% relative reduction from the 15.6% rate of the best-performing MLLM baseline on this metric. CrashLex grounds its assessment results in the deterministic execution of predefined legal rules rather than relying solely on unconstrained probabilistic generation, providing verifiable reasoning chains for rule-grounded human review.

records.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.

content.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has drastically enhanced healthcare diagnostics with automated disease detection, predictive analytics, and intelligent systems for clinical decision support. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of deep learning models hampers interpretability, clinical trust, and regulatory acceptance and raises concerns about data privacy and cybersecurity. This paper presents comprehensive experimental frameworks for developing and evaluating explainable AI models for secure healthcare diagnostics. The suggested model combines responsible data management, multimodal preprocessing, secure deep learning models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, and reproducible validation procedures in a single healthcare diagnostic pipeline. Methods of explaining, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and counterfactual analysis, were used to make the models more transparent and understandable for clinicians. At the same time, federated learning and differential privacy methods were used to securely manage highly sensitive patient data. Experimental evaluation has shown 96% classification accuracy, 94% sensitivity, and 95% specificity. These results were consistent in heterogeneous healthcare datasets. Compared to traditional black-box models, the explainability framework not only enhanced the interpretability of the results but also more accurately identified the regions relevant for diagnosis. Moreover, the secure federated learning architecture minimized privacy leakages without sacrificing the predictive performance and remained robust even when exposed to adversarial perturbations. An external evaluation also confirmed the reproducibility and generalizability of the protocols involved. This methodology offers a comprehensive and reliable foundation for deploying AI-powered diagnostics across multiple healthcare domains: radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, neurology, and precision medicine.

records.title: Beyond Accuracy: Validation, Reproducibility, and Deployment Readiness of AI in Food Safety and Quality.

content.title: Beyond Accuracy: Validation, Reproducibility, and Deployment Readiness of AI in Food Safety and Quality.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed for detecting microbial and chemical hazards in food, but laboratory accuracies are rarely reproduced in routine use. This structured narrative review examined whether reported performance is traceable, independently validated, and transferable to operational settings. Eight bibliographic databases and seven institutional routes were searched for English-language records published from January 2018 to May 2026, and we screened the records; the final corpus comprised 76 sources (53 journal articles, 9 conference papers, 2 preprints, and 12 institutional or regulatory documents). Seven primary studies supporting the quantitative evidence were appraised individually against 11 indicators, including test-set independence, external validation, and leakage control. Physical-hazard inspection and narrow-matrix spectral grading had the strongest deployment evidence, whereas microbial and chemical screening remained at laboratory or pilot scale. Among the appraised studies, the most credible estimates came from physically or temporally independent test sets, and no sensor-based study evaluated transfer to another instrument or laboratory. Deep learning showed clear advantages for image-based tasks but not consistently for small-sample spectral calibration. Adoption is limited mainly by validation design, recalibration burden, false-alarm costs, and the absence of a regulatory pathway rather than by accuracy. AI is best positioned as a screening and decision-support layer linked to confirmatory testing and human oversight.

records.title: From imaging to intelligence: AI applications in CT and MRI for hepatocellular carcinoma.
records.publisher: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association : JCMA

content.title: From imaging to intelligence: AI applications in CT and MRI for hepatocellular carcinoma.
content.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, largely due to high recurrence rates after curative treatment and poor prognosis in advanced-stage disease. Multiphasic computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) play central roles in the noninvasive diagnosis and management of HCC; however, diagnostic variability and limited sensitivity for early-stage and atypical lesions continue to pose major clinical challenges. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing medical image analysis and improving clinical decision-making in liver oncology. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-based applications for HCC imaging using CT and MRI. We discuss the roles of AI in lesion detection and segmentation, differential diagnosis and tumor classification, imaging-based biological characterization, and prediction of treatment response and prognosis. In particular, radiomics and deep learning approaches have enabled automated extraction of high-dimensional imaging features, facilitating noninvasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and heterogeneity. The integration of multimodal data, including imaging, clinical, and molecular information, further enhances predictive performance and personalized risk stratification. Despite encouraging results, most existing studies are limited by retrospective designs, heterogeneous methodologies, and insufficient external validation. Challenges related to model interpretability, data standardization, and clinical integration also remain unresolved. We highlight current limitations and future research directions, emphasizing the need for multi-center collaboration, prospective validation, and development of transparent and regulatory-compliant systems. With continued technological innovation and interdisciplinary collaboration, AI-driven imaging analysis is expected to play an increasingly important role in precision medicine and outcome optimization for patients with HCC.

records.title: Assessment, intervention, and ethical considerations of artificial intelligence for depression and suicide risk: A scoping review.

content.title: Assessment, intervention, and ethical considerations of artificial intelligence for depression and suicide risk: A scoping review.
content.abstract:
Background

Depression and suicidal behavior constitute leading causes of global disease burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers promise for improving detection, intervention, and prevention, yet no comprehensive review has simultaneously mapped AI-driven assessment, intervention, and ethical considerations across both conditions.

Objective

To systematically map AI applications for depression and suicide risk across three thematic axes: (1) assessment and diagnosis, (2) conversational AI and AI-driven interventions, and (3) ethical, equity, and regulatory considerations, and to evaluate translational maturity using a novel framework.

Methods

Following JBI scoping review methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, six databases were searched from January 2020 through March 2026. Two independent reviewers screened 5079 records using a two-stage process, yielding 2844 included studies (Cohen's kappa = 0.66). Data were extracted using a standardized charting form with AI-assisted full-text analysis.

Results

Assessment/diagnosis dominated (n = 1785), with fewer intervention studies (n = 318). Large language model-related studies rose from <1% (2020-2022) to 11.1% (2025) of included studies annually. Translational Readiness Framework classification revealed 44.8% Laboratory, 49.2% Bridge, and 6.0% Clinical stage, with intervention studies showing the highest Clinical-stage proportion (16.7% vs. 5.9% for assessment). Five cross-cutting observations emerged, including an inverted evidence pyramid and persistent cross-axis integration gap (4.4%).

Conclusion

Despite technical advances, the evidence base remains concentrated at early translational stages. The proposed Translational Readiness Framework provides a structured lens for evaluating progress and guiding research prioritization. Closing the gap between laboratory promise and clinical impact requires a shift from model-centric to patient-centric research and from benchmark performance to real-world validation.

records.title: Bone morphogenetic protein 4 meets artificial intelligence: a comprehensive review of AI-driven advances in drug discovery, structural modeling, and clinical translation.

content.title: Bone morphogenetic protein 4 meets artificial intelligence: a comprehensive review of AI-driven advances in drug discovery, structural modeling, and clinical translation.
content.abstract:
Background

Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4 (BMP4), a member of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) superfamily, plays pivotal roles in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and disease pathogenesis-including cancer, fibrosis, and fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methodologies over the past 5 years has created unprecedented opportunities for understanding and therapeutically targeting BMP4 biology at multiple scales, from atomic-resolution structure prediction to population-level clinical prognostication.

Objective

This review systematically examines the intersection of BMP4 biology and AI across three core domains: (1) AI-driven drug discovery targeting BMP4 signaling pathways, (2) deep learning-based protein structure prediction and computational modeling of BMP4 and its receptor complexes, and (3) clinical AI applications for BMP4-associated diseases.

Methods

A narrative review with systematic search elements was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, bioRxiv, and arXiv for English-language publications from 2020 to 2026, supplemented by targeted searches via Semantic Scholar. Included studies were categorized as BMP4-specific, BMP receptor/BMP-pathway-targeted, or transferable AI methodology not yet applied to BMP4.

Results

We find that AI has accelerated BMP4-related research along multiple axes, though with important caveats. AlphaFold3 and related tools have generated high-confidence predicted models of BMP4-receptor complex architecture, aspects of which were previously intractable to experimental structure determination; these predictions remain to be fully validated experimentally. ML-guided virtual screening has identified first-in-class BMP pathway (receptor) modulators for FOP, although BMP4-specific small-molecule modulators have not yet been identified computationally. Single-cell transcriptomics combined with machine learning have revealed BMP4's context-dependent roles in glioblastoma cell state transitions and cancer-associated fibroblast biology; and LASSO-Cox regression models incorporating BMP4 expression have shown promising prognostic value in pancreatic adenocarcinoma and gastric cancer, pending prospective validation. Significant gaps persist-most notably the absence of BMP4-specific de novo protein design efforts, the scarcity of large-scale training datasets for BMP4-targeted drug discovery, and the limited integration of multimodal AI approaches in BMP4 clinical research.

Conclusion

The convergence of BMP4 biology and AI represents a fertile research Frontier. While foundational tools are now in place, realizing the full translational potential of AI-augmented BMP4 research will require coordinated efforts in data generation, model development, and rigorous experimental and clinical validation. We outline priority directions for the next 5 years (approximately 2026-2031).

records.title: AI-enhanced CRISPR-Cas9 therapeutics: Advances in precision, safety, and delivery.
records.publisher: Progress in biophysics and molecular biology

content.title: AI-enhanced CRISPR-Cas9 therapeutics: Advances in precision, safety, and delivery.
content.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has transformed biomedical research and is advancing toward clinical translation. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) offers improved precision in guide RNA design, off-target prediction, and delivery optimization. This review synthesizes recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 for medical applications, covering core mechanisms, engineered variants, base and prime editors, and therapeutic applications including CAR T-cell and CAR-NK engineering, genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and regenerative medicine. Delivery strategies are evaluated with emphasis on AI-driven optimization. AI applications are highlighted across deep learning architectures for guide RNA design, AI-designed nucleases such as OpenCRISPR-1, structure-guided and AI-assisted design of compact high-fidelity SaCas9 variants, reinforcement learning for pipeline optimization, and roles in CAR T-cell therapy and safety assessment. Safety challenges are examined, including off-target effects, chromosomal rearrangements, immunogenicity, and regulatory concerns. Future directions emphasize multi-scale modeling, explainable AI, clinical validation, and integration with synthetic biology, single-cell sequencing, organoids, and nanomaterials. The convergence of AI and CRISPR-Cas9 holds substantial potential for personalized medicine.

records.title: AI-Enabled Animal Behavior Analysis for Translational Pharmacology and Therapeutic Discovery.

content.title: AI-Enabled Animal Behavior Analysis for Translational Pharmacology and Therapeutic Discovery.
content.abstract: Animal behavior is a critical endpoint in preclinical pharmacology, toxicology, and therapeutic discovery, yet conventional behavioral scoring remains labor-intensive, low-dimensional, and difficult to reproduce across laboratories. Artificial intelligence (AI) can now quantify behavior from video with greater spatial, temporal, and phenotypic resolution. This review summarizes how object detection, markerless pose estimation, unsupervised behavioral segmentation, foundation models, and autonomous analysis agents are reshaping behavioral phenotyping. General-purpose object detectors rapidly localize and track animals, whereas open-source pose-estimation tools extend measurement beyond centroid tracking to body-part trajectories and fine motor patterns; paired with supervised classifiers, they have matched human scoring and exceeded some commercial systems. Technical accuracy alone does not establish behavioral construct validity or pharmacological validity. Unsupervised methods such as Motion Sequencing represent drug responses and disease-model phenotypes as structured changes in behavioral states rather than only as predefined endpoints, providing high-dimensional fingerprints of pharmacological action. Segmentation and tracking foundation models may reduce annotation burden but require validation across species, strain, sex, apparatus, and paradigm. AI agents may assist with literature review, code generation, analysis auditing, and figure production but must remain within transparent, human-supervised workflows. In behavioral pharmacology, pose estimation is established as a measurement method and emerging as a drug-effect endpoint, supervised classification and unsupervised segmentation are emerging, and foundation models and agents remain prospective. AI-enabled behavioral analysis can become a reproducible phenotyping layer for drug discovery and toxicology if researchers adopt open pipelines, rigorous validation, and reporting standards, rather than replacing one opaque measurement system with another.

records.title: Artificial intelligence-based voice biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of neurological diseases: current evidence, limitations, and clinical perspectives.

content.title: Artificial intelligence-based voice biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of neurological diseases: current evidence, limitations, and clinical perspectives.
content.abstract:
Background

Early diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of neurological diseases remain major clinical challenges because current diagnostic approaches are often expensive, invasive, or insufficiently sensitive to detect early functional changes. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach for analyzing voice and speech as non-invasive digital biomarkers capable of capturing subtle alterations associated with neurological dysfunction.

Methods

This narrative review analyzed studies published between 2015 and 2026 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The review critically examines the limitations of current neurological diagnostic methods, summarizes the available evidence on AI-based voice and speech biomarkers, discusses machine learning and deep learning approaches applied to speech analysis, and evaluates the methodological, ethical, and regulatory challenges that currently limit their clinical implementation.

Results

Current evidence indicates that AI-based voice biomarkers have considerable potential for screening, diagnostic support, and longitudinal monitoring of neurological disorders, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, and other neurodegenerative conditions. Several studies report high diagnostic performance under controlled experimental settings. However, substantial heterogeneity in study design, sample size, languages, speech acquisition protocols, validation strategies, and reporting standards limits direct comparison between studies and hinders clinical translation. External validation and prospective multicenter studies remain scarce.

Conclusion

AI-based voice analysis represents a promising, scalable, and non-invasive complement to conventional neurological assessment, with particular potential for remote screening and disease monitoring. Nevertheless, current evidence does not yet support routine clinical implementation. Future progress will depend on standardized speech acquisition protocols, robust external validation across diverse populations, explainable AI models, and regulatory frameworks capable of ensuring safety, reproducibility, and clinical reliability.

records.title: Explainable fMRI decoding reveals neurobiological signatures of emotional arousal complementary to traditional analyses.

content.title: Explainable fMRI decoding reveals neurobiological signatures of emotional arousal complementary to traditional analyses.
content.abstract: Objective.Understanding how emotional arousal is represented in the brain is fundamental for elucidating affective regulation and its alterations in autism spectrum disorder. Classical neuroimaging approaches, such as the general linear model (GLM), have provided important insights into emotional processing. However, the extent to which data-driven decoding and traditional model-based analyses provide complementary information about emotional arousal remains unclear.Approach.We introduce an explainable artificial intelligence framework that combines the lightweight functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) decoder (fMRINet) with Deep Learning Important FeaTures to derive data-driven neurobiological signatures of emotional arousal. The framework enables interpretation of spatiotemporal neural contributions during emotional processing. We applied the framework to fMRI data acquired while neurotypically and autistic participants viewed naturalistic emotional videos and compared the resulting signatures with categorical and parametric GLM analyses.Main results.The framework identified distinct spatiotemporal neurobiological signatures associated with emotional arousal. Neurotypical participants engaged a distributed perceptual-limbic-prefrontal network under high arousal and frontoparietal executive regions under low arousal. In contrast, autistic participants exhibited a more spatially restricted and posterior-biased pattern under high arousal, with reduced ventromedial prefrontal and limbic contributions, while low-arousal patterns resembled typically developing, suggesting preserved executive mechanisms during low-arousal processing. The GLM analyses revealed partly convergent and partly distinct findings: categorical GLM detected no significant group differences, whereas parametric GLM identified widespread cortical-subcortical modulation in neurotypical individuals and cerebellar-restricted effects in autistic, consistent with compensatory reliance on motor-timing circuits.Significance. The proposed framework provides an interpretable, data-driven perspective on emotional processing and reveals neurobiologically plausible patterns consistent with existing literature. Together, the explainable decoding and GLM results highlight complementary aspects of emotional arousal processing, suggesting that explainable decoding approaches may provide additional insights alongside traditional model-based neuroimaging analyses.
