Through a systematic evaluation of recent literature, we examine studies focused on the development, validation, or critical appraisal of AI-driven technologies for ICH care. Our analysis encompasses automated neuroimaging, computer-assisted surgical navigation, brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), prognostic modeling, and fundamental research into disease mechanisms. AI has demonstrated performance comparable to that of clinical experts in automating hematoma segmentation, predicting complications such as hematoma expansion, and refining surgical planning via augmented reality. Furthermore, BCIs present innovative therapeutic avenues for motor rehabilitation. However, the translation of these technological advances into routine clinical practice is impeded by substantial challenges, including data heterogeneity, model opacity ("black-box" issues), workflow integration barriers, regulatory ambiguities, and ethical concerns surrounding accountability and algorithmic bias. The integration of AI into ICH care signifies a paradigm shift from standardized treatment protocols toward dynamic, precision medicine. Realizing this vision necessitates interdisciplinary collaboration to engineer robust, generalizable, and interpretable AI systems. Key priorities include the establishment of large-scale multimodal data repositories, the advancement of explainable AI (XAI) frameworks, the execution of rigorous prospective clinical trials to validate efficacy, and the implementation of adaptive regulatory and ethical guidelines. By systematically addressing these barriers, AI can evolve from a mere analytical tool into an indispensable clinical partner, ultimately optimizing patient outcomes.

records.title: Artificial intelligence based predictive models for early sepsis detection in intensive care units: a scoping review.

content.title: Artificial intelligence based predictive models for early sepsis detection in intensive care units: a scoping review.
content.abstract:
Background

Early detection of sepsis in intensive care units remains a major clinical challenge. Artificial intelligence based predictive models have emerged as promising tools to support early identification of sepsis, yet their clinical readiness and methodological robustness remain heterogeneous.

Objective

To map and critically synthesize the available evidence on artificial intelligence based predictive models for early sepsis detection in intensive care units.

Methods

A scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA ScR framework. Multiple databases were systematically searched to identify studies developing or validating artificial intelligence based models for early sepsis detection in adult intensive care settings. Data were extracted on study design, data sources, model type, prediction horizon, validation strategies, and reported performance.

Results

Thirty seven studies were included. Most models were developed using retrospective electronic health record data and relied on machine learning techniques, with limited external validation. Reported performance varied widely, and few studies addressed clinical implementation, interpretability, or integration into real time workflows.

Conclusions

Although artificial intelligence based models show potential for early sepsis detection, substantial gaps remain regarding external validation, clinical integration, and real world applicability. Future research should prioritize methodological transparency and implementation focused evaluation.

records.title: Harnessing big data and artificial intelligence in transfusion medicine: Opportunities for precision, safety and efficiency.

content.title: Harnessing big data and artificial intelligence in transfusion medicine: Opportunities for precision, safety and efficiency.
content.abstract: Transfusion medicine generates enormous volumes of data across the vein-to-vein continuum, spanning donor characteristics, laboratory testing, component manufacturing, logistics and recipient outcomes. The emergence of big data infrastructures, coupled with artificial intelligence (AI), offers a transformative opportunity to harness this information for safer, more efficient and better personalized transfusion practices. This narrative review outlines current and potential applications of AI and machine learning (ML) at each phase of the big data pipeline in transfusion medicine, including data collection, wrangling and harmonization, validation, feature engineering, analysis, publication and knowledge mobilization. We discuss how AI-enabled methods-such as natural language processing to extract variables, anomaly detection for product quality, supervised models to predict risks, federated analysis for collaboration, and forecasting algorithms to optimize inventory and logistics-may address longstanding challenges related to data fragmentation, unstructured documentation and labour-intensive manual validation. We emphasize critical risks and limitations of applying AI to big data analytics and discuss mitigation through robust governance, performance monitoring, fairness audits, cybersecurity measures and transparent human oversight. We end by offering key recommendations and future directions, highlighting that strategic, equitable and ethically sound implementation will be essential to realizing benefits and ensuring trust in an increasingly data-driven transfusion ecosystem.

records.title: AI-Driven Innovations for Quality Control and Standardization: Future Strategies in Adipose-Derived Stem Cell Manufacturing.

content.title: AI-Driven Innovations for Quality Control and Standardization: Future Strategies in Adipose-Derived Stem Cell Manufacturing.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), is increasingly transforming the study, manufacturing, and clinical translation of adipose-derived stem/stromal cells (ADSCs). ADSC-based therapies face persistent challenges related to donor variability, heterogeneous cell populations, limited standardization of culture protocols, and the need for robust quality control (QC) and potency assessment under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) conditions. This review discusses how AI-driven approaches can support the ADSC pipeline from donor and tissue pre-screening, through isolation and expansion, to differentiation and batch release decisions. We highlight major methodological advances in computer vision and label-free imaging for monitoring morphology, confluency, proliferation, senescence, and contamination, as well as AI-assisted optimization strategies for culture parameters and differentiation protocols. In addition, we examine the growing role of multi-omics integration (transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and secretomics) combined with ML to predict functional potency, stratify donors, and identify biomarkers associated with therapeutic efficacy. Finally, we address current limitations, including data scarcity, inter-laboratory variability, model interpretability, and regulatory requirements, and outline future perspectives such as closed-loop bioprocess control, foundation models, and federated learning frameworks. Overall, AI offers a powerful toolkit to improve the reproducibility, safety, and scalability of ADSC manufacturing and to accelerate the development of standardized, data-driven regenerative medicine products.

records.title: Effects of curcumin supplementation on homocysteine levels: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Effects of curcumin supplementation on homocysteine levels: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Homocysteine (Hcy) is an established cardiovascular risk factor, and dietary modulation via nutraceuticals represents a promising preventive strategy. Curcumin, a bioactive polyphenol from Curcuma longa L., exhibits pleiotropic biological activities; however, its capacity to reduce circulating Hcy remains uncertain.

Objectives

To systematically evaluate the effect of curcumin supplementation on Hcy levels.

Methods

Eight databases were searched from inception to November 2025 for RCTs investigating curcumin and Hcy outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2.0. A random-effects model was applied.

Results

Three randomized controlled trials (RCT) with a total of 110 subjects were included in this study. Due to physiologically implausible Hcy values in one study (Rezaei 2024), the primary meta-analysis was restricted to two RCTs with interpretable data (Ghaffari 2017 and Campbell 2019). The results of Meta-analysis showed that compared with the control group, the pooled standardized mean difference SMD = -2.08, 95% confidence interval was -4.67 to 0.51, P = 0.116, there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups. There was a high degree of heterogeneity among the included studies (I2 = 91.6%, P = 0.001). Risk of bias assessment (RoB 2.0) rated one study as low risk, one as some concerns, and one as high risk (selective reporting). Sensitivity analysis that included the study with implausible data (Rezaei 2024) gave a similar non-significant pooled estimate (SMD = -1.23, 95% CI -2.82 to 0.36, P = 0.13; I2 = 91.9%).

Conclusion

Current RCT evidence does not support a statistically significant Hcy-lowering effect of curcumin. The overall certainty of evidence is very low due to small sample size, extreme heterogeneity, and risk of bias. Curcumin should not be recommended as a standalone intervention for lowering Hcy. Its potential role, if any, requires confirmation in well-powered trials using optimized, high-bioavailability formulations.

records.title: Global research trends in m<sup>6</sup>A demethylases and cancer: a bibliometric and visualization analysis.

content.title: Global research trends in m<sup>6</sup>A demethylases and cancer: a bibliometric and visualization analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

The role of m6A demethylases in tumorigenesis has garnered increasing attention; however, the global research landscape and thematic evolution in this field remain to be fully elucidated. This study aims to investigate the dynamic scientific development of the m6A demethylase-tumor field through bibliometric analysis.

Methods

Literature pertaining to m6A demethylases and tumors published between 2015 and 2025 was retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) database. Quantitative and visual analyses were subsequently performed using the bibliometrix package in R. A cross-database sensitivity analysis using PubMed was conducted to assess whether the descriptive patterns were generally consistent across databases.

Results

A total of 761 eligible publications were included in this study. The field has experienced rapid growth since 2020, with an average annual growth rate of 50.92%. China and the United States emerged as the leading contributors in terms of publication output. Research efforts were concentrated at institutions such as Sun Yat-sen University, forming a highly productive collaborative cluster centered on LI YANG. Keyword analysis revealed that gastric cancer, liver cancer, and colorectal cancer constituted the core cancer types examined. The research focus has evolved from early investigations of basic mechanisms to the tumor immune microenvironment, therapeutic resistance, and prognostic evaluation. The annual trend and geographical distribution obtained by PubMed sensitivity analysis are consistent with the direction of WoSCC results, suggesting that the main conclusions have not changed substantially because of database selection.

Conclusion

Research in the m6A demethylase-tumor field is advancing rapidly. Current research efforts are predominantly directed toward the remodeling of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by demethylases and the underlying mechanisms of therapeutic resistance. These findings provide a valuable direction and a novel perspective for further investigation of m6A demethylases in oncology.

records.title: Effects of visual art therapy on cognitive function in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Effects of visual art therapy on cognitive function in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To systematically review the evidence on the effects of visual art therapy on global cognitive function in older adults, and to examine its impact on verbal fluency, naming ability, and activities of daily living.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, Wanfang Database, and VIP Database for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published from database inception to July 2026. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4 and Stata 15.0. The primary outcome was global cognitive function, and secondary outcomes included the Verbal Fluency Test (VFT), the Boston Naming Test (BNT), and activities of daily living. Fixed-effects or random-effects models were used according to heterogeneity, and subgroup analyses were conducted.

Results

A total of 10 randomized controlled trials involving 628 older participants were included, of whom 318 were allocated to visual art therapy and 310 to control conditions. Meta-analysis showed that visual art therapy significantly improved global cognitive function in older adults (SMD = 0.39, 95% CI: 0.23-0.54, P < 0.00001). For secondary outcomes, compared with control groups, statistically significant improvements were observed in verbal fluency (MD = 1.21, 95% CI: 0.12-2.29, P = 0.03), naming ability (MD = 1.74, 95% CI: 0.20-3.28, P = 0.03), and activities of daily living (SMD = -0.36, 95% CI: -0.62 to -0.10, P = 0.006) in the visual art therapy group. However, the evidence is based on only two or three studies and was rated as low or very low certainty. Subgroup analyses indicated larger effect sizes for interventions delivered 13-24 times, with 30-40 minutes per session, and among older adults with mild cognitive impairment, given the limited number of studies per subgroup, these findings are exploratory and should be interpreted with caution.

Conclusion

Visual art therapy can significantly enhance global cognitive function in older adults and confers additional benefits on language functions and activities of daily living. As a safe, non-invasive, non-pharmacological intervention, visual art therapy may serve as an effective adjunctive approach for managing cognitive decline and daily functioning in the older population.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261337553, identifier CRD420261337553.

records.title: Clinical effects of probiotic supplementation on depressive symptom severity in adults with depressive disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Clinical effects of probiotic supplementation on depressive symptom severity in adults with depressive disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Probiotic supplementation has been investigated as a potential adjunctive treatment for depressive disorders, but its clinical efficacy and safety remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of probiotics on depressive symptom severity, clinical response, remission, treatment discontinuation, and adverse events in adults with clinically diagnosed depressive disorders.

Methods

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 8, 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating orally administered probiotics against placebo or another non-probiotic control were included. Continuous outcomes were summarized as standardized mean differences (SMDs) using Hedges' g, and dichotomous outcomes as risk ratios (RRs), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Random-effects models used restricted maximum likelihood estimation with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q, I2, and τ2, and robustness was examined using leave-one-out sensitivity analysis.

Results

Nine RCTs involving 460 participants were included. Probiotic supplementation was associated with a modest reduction in depressive symptom severity (SMD, -0.43; 95% CI, -0.73 to -0.12; I2 = 46.8%; τ2 = 0.069). The 95% prediction interval ranged from -1.10 to 0.25. Leave-one-out estimates ranged from -0.52 to -0.38, with all 95% CIs excluding zero. No significant effect modification was detected across formulation, dose, duration, treatment context, diagnostic population, or outcome-rater subgroups. Clinical response and remission were available from one trial and remained inconclusive (RR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.32-1.77; and RR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.08-2.19, respectively). All-cause discontinuation did not differ clearly between groups (seven RCTs; RR, 1.15; 95% CI, 0.67-1.98). Adverse-event evidence was limited and inconsistently reported.

Conclusion

Probiotic supplementation may modestly reduce depressive symptom severity, particularly as an adjunct to established treatment. However, the prediction interval included the null, and evidence regarding clinical response, remission, and safety remained inconclusive. Larger, adequately powered RCTs with standardized clinically meaningful outcomes and strain-specific reporting are required.

records.title: Research progress and trends of gut microbiota and lung injury: a bibliometric and visualization analysis based on two databases (2015-2026).

content.title: Research progress and trends of gut microbiota and lung injury: a bibliometric and visualization analysis based on two databases (2015-2026).
content.abstract:
Background

Gut microbiota has emerged as an important regulator of lung injury, but the field's research structure, hotspots and emerging directions remain unclear. This study mapped the development and knowledge landscape of gut microbiota and lung injury research.

Methods

Publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus from 2015 to May 2026 were analyzed using VOSviewer, CiteSpace and Bibliometrix.

Results

Publication output increased markedly, particularly after 2019, with China and Fudan University leading national and institutional contributions, respectively. Frontiers in Immunology was a major publication and citation hub. Keyword patterns highlighted inflammation, the gut-lung axis, immune regulation, mouse models and sepsis.

Conclusion

Major research themes included microbiota-mediated regulation of pulmonary immunity, the protective effects of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and microbiota-targeted interventions involving probiotics and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). The field remains dominated by mechanistic and preclinical studies, underscoring the need for standardized methods and clinical validation.

records.title: Integrating AI-Driven Diagnostics in Arrhythmia Care to Enhance Patient Outcomes: A Narrative Review.

content.title: Integrating AI-Driven Diagnostics in Arrhythmia Care to Enhance Patient Outcomes: A Narrative Review.
content.abstract: International morbidity and mortality are led by cardiovascular disease, specifically arrhythmias. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) can promote earlier identification and, therefore, provide personalized clinical judgments sooner, which can avert these consequences. AI is mainly used in diagnostics, prognostics, and decision support through test interpretations (electrocardiographs (ECGs) and MRI scans) and computing hidden characteristics to utilize a personalized plan rather than a population-based one. While such technology is available in hospitals, some functions are also being integrated into smart wearable devices. These wearable devices allow for continuous monitoring rather than limiting it to in-hospital settings, thus making it easier to enable an earlier diagnosis. However, certain arrhythmias, such as asymptomatic arrhythmias, can go unnoticed by AI. Additionally, there are questions regarding data transparency, privacy, and the financial burden of utilizing and managing AI in medical settings.

records.title: Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence.

content.title: Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence.
content.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

records.title: Exercise interventions and multidimensional cognitive function in esports players: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Exercise interventions and multidimensional cognitive function in esports players: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background and objective

Esports places stringent demands on participants in terms of neural information processing speed, real-time decision-making precision, and cognitive stability. The coexistence of prolonged sedentary training patterns and sustained high-intensity mental workload has rendered the maintenance of cognitive function in esports populations an urgent scientific concern. This study employs systematic review and meta-analysis methods to quantitatively synthesize the effects of exercise interventions on multidimensional cognitive function in esports players, with the aim of providing evidence-based references for the scientific training of esports athletes.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and Scopus from database inception to May 3, 2026, to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated physical activity interventions among esports players. Two independent researchers completed literature screening and data extraction. The RoB 2.0 tool was used to assess risk of bias, and standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were synthesized using a random-effects model.

Results

A total of 5,298 records were identified through database searching, and 10 randomized controlled trials involving 503 participants were ultimately included. Regarding cognitive speed, exercise intervention significantly reduced players' reaction time (SMD = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.50-1.18), with subgroup analysis indicating that VR/exergame interventions yielded a numerically higher effect size (SMD = 1.01) compared to traditional aerobic exercise (SMD = 0.64). Regarding operational accuracy, the intervention effect was robust and highly consistent across conditions (SMD = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.40-0.76, I2 = 0%), remaining stable across both intervention media (traditional 0.53 vs. VR 0.64) and intervention duration (acute 0.57 vs. long-term 0.59). Regarding executive function and memory, the pooled effect size after excluding high-risk studies was SMD = 0.63 (95% CI: 0.36-0.91, I2 = 0%), suggesting a robust promoting effect of exercise intervention on higher-order cognitive function. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that core outcome effects remained significant after removing sources of heterogeneity, and Egger's test indicated no significant publication bias for the accuracy outcome (p = 0.54).

Conclusion

Current evidence suggests that exercise intervention is a potentially effective approach for improving multidimensional cognitive function in esports players, with positive effects observed across cognitive processing speed, operational precision, and executive function and memory. VR/exergame interventions showed a numerically larger effect size for cognitive processing speed compared with traditional exercise modalities; however, this difference should be interpreted cautiously due to the exploratory nature of subgroup analyses. Future esports training systems may consider incorporating structured exercise interventions into routine training programs, with the aim of maintaining players' cognitive health while exploring feasible pathways for extending career longevity.

Systematic review registration

www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero, identifier [CRD420261385557].

records.title: Is hands-on learning still necessary in the age of AI? A thematic review.

content.title: Is hands-on learning still necessary in the age of AI? A thematic review.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly entering design education and influencing how students engage in the design process. Existing studies have widely explored the potential of AI for creative production and improving design efficiency. Less attention has been paid to whether hands-on learning is still necessary in the age of AI.

Methods

This study adopted a thematic review approach to examine changes in the role of hands-on learning in AI-supported design education and its educational value. The review was based on 32 peer-reviewed studies retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus.

Results

The reviewed literature suggests that AI does not simply replace hands-on learning but changes how it may take place. Two interrelated forms can be distinguished: Embodied Hands-on, based on the body, tools, and materials, and Cognitive Hands-on, based on language, judgement, and human -AI iteration. Both share a cycle of action, feedback, reflection, and refinement, but their educational roles are not equivalent. The review also identifies concerns including the compression of learning processes, dependence on AI-generated outcomes, and an increasing emphasis on evaluation.

Discussion

This study proposes a process-oriented framework for understanding how Embodied Hands-on and Cognitive Hands-on may relate to creative thinking, design judgement, and student agency. The findings suggest that design literacy may increasingly involve critical evaluation, metacognitive regulation, and decision-making in human -AI collaboration.

records.title: The relationship between green space and myopia in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: The relationship between green space and myopia in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To investigate the effect of green space exposure on the risk of myopia in children and adolescents.

Methods

Studies on the relationship between green space and myopia in children and adolescents published before October 1, 2024, were retrieved from five electronic databases: web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, EBSCOhost, ScienceDirect and Cochrane Library. A systematic review was conducted to summarize the relevant articles, followed by a meta-analysis.

Results

A total of 11 studies were included in the systematic review, encompassing 2,224,332 participants aged 6-22 years. Of these, 6 studies were incorporated into the meta-analysis. Most studies indicated that increased green space is associated with a reduced risk of myopia. The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) showed a negative correlation with the prevalence of myopia in children and adolescents (cross-sectional studies: OR = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.94-0.96, I 2= 37.2%, P = 0.158; cohort studies: OR = 0.91, 95% CI: 0.91-0.91, I 2= 88.9%, P < 0.001). NDVI within school boundaries and a 500-meter buffer zone had a more significant effect on myopia prevention (within school boundaries: OR = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.77-0.99, P = 0.206; 500-meter buffer zone around schools: OR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.94-0.97, P = 0.098; 1,000-meter buffer zone around schools: OR = 0.94, 95% CI: 0.92-0.97, P = 0.315) (within school boundaries: OR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.94-0.98, P = 0.066; 500-meter buffer zone around schools: OR = 0.90, 95% CI: 0.90-0.91, P = 0.053).

Conclusion

Increased exposure to green spaces has a beneficial effect on reducing the risk of myopia in children and adolescents. For every 0.1 increase in the NDVI, the prevalence of myopia decreases. Furthermore, the prevention and control of myopia are more effective within school boundaries and in the surrounding 500-meter buffer zone. Therefore, it is recommended that schools and relevant government authorities focus on enhancing vegetation coverage within school grounds and around areas where students frequently engage in activities, thereby providing stronger environmental support for myopia prevention in children and adolescents. However, potential publication bias cannot be excluded given the limited number of included studies; therefore, the pooled estimates should be interpreted with caution.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251153654, PROSPERO: CRD420251153654.

records.title: Effects of Stand-Alone Digital Lifestyle Interventions on Weight-Related Outcomes in Adults With Overweight or Obesity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

content.title: Effects of Stand-Alone Digital Lifestyle Interventions on Weight-Related Outcomes in Adults With Overweight or Obesity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Obesity is a major global health concern, and scalable digital solutions are urgently needed. While digital lifestyle interventions (DLSIs) have shown promise, prior meta-analyses often included hybrid formats with human support, limiting insights into the effectiveness of fully digital interventions.

Objective

This study aimed to evaluate the independent effects of standalone DLSIs-defined as interventions delivered exclusively via digital platforms without in-person or adjunctive support-on anthropometric and dietary outcomes in adults with overweight or obesity.

Methods

We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from inception through March 4, 2026. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating stand-alone DLSIs in adults with overweight or obesity. Interventions were included if they targeted diet or physical activity exclusively through digital platforms. We included fully automated, asynchronous, or one-to-many synchronous systems without individualized support. Studies involving hybrid interventions, including one-to-one synchronous human interaction, nonadult populations, or non-RCT designs, were excluded. Two independent reviewers performed study selection and data extraction. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool (Cochrane Bias Methods Group). Meta-analysis used a random-effects model with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method, and heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach.

Results

A total of 19 RCTs involving 3556 participants were included. Stand-alone DLSIs significantly improved anthropometric outcomes compared to controls (standardized mean difference 0.26, 95% CI 0.14-0.38; 95% prediction interval [PI] -0.16 to 0.68; P<.001; 19 studies; n=3556; I2=56.1%), corresponding to an additional weight loss ranging from 2.62 kg to 6.55 kg, depending on the baseline body weight. Significant improvements were also found in dietary outcomes (standardized mean difference 0.26, 95% CI 0.04-0.48; 95% PI -0.29 to 0.81; P=.008; 8 studies; n=1365; I2=57.5%). Subgroup analyses for anthropometric outcomes revealed significant differences only by control group type (P<.001), with waitlist controls showing the largest effect. For dietary outcomes, no significant subgroup differences were found (P>.05). While most studies showed a low risk of bias, substantial statistical heterogeneity was observed in some outcomes. Consequently, the certainty of evidence for both outcomes was rated as moderate.

Conclusions

This review is innovative as it is the first to isolate the pure efficacy of stand-alone DLSIs by excluding synchronous human support. Our findings provide moderate-certainty evidence that these tools are effective for weight management and dietary improvement without human intervention. While stand-alone DLSIs offer a highly scalable, cost-effective first-step intervention, the PIs included zero, and substantial heterogeneity was observed, suggesting that benefits may vary across settings. Future research should identify user characteristics that maximize engagement with unguided digital tools.

records.title: Association between BDNF and postoperative cognitive dysfunction across surgical stages: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Association between BDNF and postoperative cognitive dysfunction across surgical stages: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract: Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) is a frequent complication after surgery, particularly among older adults, and its underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a key regulator of neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity, and has been implicated in POCD but published findings are inconsistent. We therefore performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the association between perioperative BDNF levels and POCD across surgical time points. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched for observational studies that reported perioperative BDNF levels in patients with and without POCD. Two reviewers independently extraction data and assessed study quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Statistical analyses were conducted in RevMan 5.3, with mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for absolute BDNF levels and perioperative changes (ΔBDNF) at preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative stages. Six studies including 135 patients with POCD and 247 without POCD met the inclusion criteria. The fixed-effects meta-analysis showed lower intraoperative BDNF levels in the POCD group (MD = -5.62, 95% CI[-8.95, -2.29], P = 0.0009; I 2 = 0%). Similarly, intraoperative ΔBDNF was reduced in the POCD group under a fixed-effects meta-model (MD = -9.73, 95% CI[-16.08, -3.38], P = 0.003; I 2 = 0%). The subgroup analysis indicated that the type of surgery may contribute to the high heterogeneity observed in 24-h postoperative BDNF and in 24-h postoperative ΔBDNF. These findings suggest that intraoperative BDNF levels and their dynamic changes may serve as preliminary exploratory biomarker for POCD. The intraoperative phase appears to be a critical window for BDNF monitoring, yet prospective cohort studies are urgently needed to externally validate its uesfulness for screening patients at high risk of POCD before clinical implementation. Current evidence remains preliminary, since only six small observational studies were included and substantial statistical heterogeneity was present in multiple postoperative subgroup analyses. Systematic review registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251265921.

records.title: Vaginal and endometrial microbiota dysbiosis in patients with chronic endometritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

content.title: Vaginal and endometrial microbiota dysbiosis in patients with chronic endometritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Chronic endometritis (CE), a persistent inflammatory condition of the endometrial lining, is clinically linked with adverse reproductive outcomes. It is currently hypothesized to be associated with infection, and is often treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. However, the specific microbial alterations remain poorly defined due to heterogeneous findings.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched for studies published up to July 2025. Studies were included if they compared CE patients to non-CE controls and analyzed vaginal or endometrial microbiota. Standardized mean difference (SMD) for alpha-diversity, odds ratio (OR) for microbial detection rates, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Qualitative syntheses of beta-diversity and microbial abundance profiles were also performed.

Result

Twenty-two studies (n = 1274 CE patients, n = 1109 controls) were included. Alpha-diversity indices showed no significant differences for both vaginal and endometrial microbiota. However, a subgroup analysis revealed a significant upregulation in endometrial Chao1 indices in 16S V4 sequencing studies (SMD = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.06 to 0.70, I 2 = 0). Beta-diversity findings were inconsistent, though three endometrial studies reported significant intergroup differences. Qualitative synthesis revealed a decrease in Lactobacillus and an increase in opportunistic pathogens, including Gardnerella and Sphingomonas. Pooled analysis of microbial detection rates showed significantly higher prevalence for Enterococcus (OR = 4.93, 95% CI: 2.13 to 11.39, I 2 = 48%) and Ureaplasma (OR = 6.30, 95% CI: 2.53 to 15.68, I 2 = 0%) in CE patients.

Conclusion

CE is associated with dysbiosis of the vaginal and endometrial microbiota, characterized by a shift from beneficial commensals to pathogenic microbes. This dysbiosis may contribute to an altered the intrauterine immune microenvironment.

Systematic review registration

PROSPERO https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251115587, identifier CRD420251115587.

records.title: The impact of using dexmedetomidine during surgery on the postoperative survival of cancer patients: a meta-analysis and systematic review of real-world studies.

content.title: The impact of using dexmedetomidine during surgery on the postoperative survival of cancer patients: a meta-analysis and systematic review of real-world studies.
content.abstract:
Background

Perioperative stress and immunosuppression may influence tumor recurrence and long-term survival in cancer patients. Dexmedetomidine, a widely used anesthetic adjunct, remains controversial regarding its impact on postoperative prognosis. Some studies suggest it may attenuate immunosuppression, whereas others point to a potential tumor-promoting effect. This meta-analysis aimed to synthesize evidence from real-world studies and evaluate the association between intraoperative dexmedetomidine use and post-surgical survival in cancer patients.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, and Wanfang Database from inception to April 2026 for real-world observational studies examining the association between intraoperative dexmedetomidine use and postoperative survival in cancer patients. The primary outcomes were overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS). Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled for survival endpoints. Sensitivity analyses tested the robustness of the results, and subgroup analyses were performed according to study characteristics. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots, Begg's test, and Egger's test. All statistical analyses were conducted with Stata 15.0.

Results

Eight studies comprising 4,613 patients were included. The meta-analysis revealed no statistically significant association between intraoperative dexmedetomidine use and postoperative OS (HR = 0.95, 95% CI (0.72, 1.24), P = 0.685) or RFS (HR = 0.85, 95% CI (0.61, 1.20), P = 0.363). Subgroup analyses suggested that dexmedetomidine might improve OS in colorectal cancer patients, but no such difference was observed in renal cell carcinoma or other tumor types. Across different sample sizes and geographic regions, dexmedetomidine use was not significantly associated with OS.

Conclusion

This meta-analysis of real-world evidence indicates that intraoperative dexmedetomidine use is not statistically significantly associated with OS and RFS in cancer patients. Although the subgroup finding for colorectal cancer hints at a possible survival benefits, the overall evidence does not support routine dexmedetomidine administration for improving long-term oncological outcomes. Given the limited number of included studies and potential confounding factors, causal inferences should be avoided. Large-scale, prospective real-world studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261370773.

records.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
content.abstract:
Background

Dietary protein supplements are commonly consumed to support increases in lean body mass among healthy adults engaged in resistance training (RT). Although whey protein has been extensively investigated, plant-based protein supplements have emerged as a viable alternative for individuals who avoid animal-derived products.

Methods

The present study aims to evaluate, through a systematic review and meta-analysis, the effects of plant-based versus whey protein supplementation on body composition in untrained adults (18-59 years) undergoing RT, using Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). The systematic review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251145410). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, identifying 5 studies that met the inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis and meta-analysis.

Results

When combined with RT, both plant-based and whey protein supplementation were associated with improvements in lean body mass (LBM) and body fat mass (BFM), with no significant between-group differences observed.

Conclusions

Thus, soy- and pea-based protein supplements may support favorable body composition changes in adults initiating RT and could be considered practical nutritional options for individuals seeking alternatives to whey protein. Regarding chia-based protein, the available evidence is currently limited to a single study that did not demonstrate significant changes in lean body mass; therefore, firm conclusions regarding its efficacy cannot be drawn at this time.

records.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Gomes, M, Costa, M, Pezarat-Correia, P, and Mendonca, GV. Lower-body strength and hypertrophy adaptations in response to concurrent training in trained young males. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined the interference effect of concurrent training (CT) on maximal and explosive strength and muscle morphology in trained young males. Thirty subjects were randomly assigned to endurance training (E), resistance training (R), or CT for 11 weeks. The intervention comprised 2 mesocycles: weeks 1-5 emphasizing maximal strength, and weeks 6-11 targeting explosive strength. Assessments were conducted at baseline, mid-training, and post-training, and included leg-press maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC), rate of force development (RFD), countermovement jump kinetics, and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area and pennation angle. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction increased only in the R group (18.4 ± 10.2%, p = 0.015). Peak RFD improved in both R (31.8 ± 23.2%) and CT (23.1 ± 27.9%), although with distinct time courses: R improved progressively across both mesocycles, whereas CT improved only during the second. Early-phase RFD (0-50 ms) increased in the R group from mid-training onward, whereas the CT group improved only from mid- to post-training (38.3 ± 40.4%, p = 0.021), accompanied by greater quadriceps electromyographic activity (p < 0.05). No changes in RFD were observed in E during training. Countermovement jump positive impulse improved in both R (12.7 ± 9.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 8.3%, p < 0.05), with no evidence of interference in jump-related explosive performance. Cross-sectional area increased in both R (17.0 ± 13.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 9.4%, p < 0.05). Pennation angle increased in CT (10.1 ± 12.9%) and R (18.6 ± 15.1%). These findings indicate that, although CT may limit MVIC development and delay early-phase RFD adaptations, it does not hinder explosive performance when resistance training is oriented toward rapid-strength development. Thus, CT can be effectively implemented in trained individuals when resistance training is periodized to emphasize neural-driven explosive or hypertrophy-related adaptations.

records.title: Regional lean mass, bone mineral measures, and estimated leg press 1-RM in resistance-trained males.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Regional lean mass, bone mineral measures, and estimated leg press 1-RM in resistance-trained males.
content.abstract:
Background

Regional lean mass, bone mineral content (BMC), and strength are related in young men, but it is less clear how much these relationships simply reflect shared body and skeletal size in resistance-trained individuals. We therefore examined broad regional associations between lean mass and bone measures, together with selected bone and function relationships, with particular attention to body size.

Methods

This cross-sectional secondary analysis used baseline data from 44 resistance-trained males from a previous four group trial. Whole body dual energy X ray absorptiometry (DXA) provided broad upper body and lower body lean mass measures, BMC, projected bone area, and areal bone mineral density (BMD). We examined associations using Pearson correlations and linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age and height were considered alongside body mass, projected area, and allometric models. Benjamini Hochberg correction across all 18 adjusted cross-sectional tests was prioritized.

Results

Regional lean mass was positively associated with several BMC outcomes in models adjusted for age and height, including arm BMC (standardized β = 0.605), rib BMC (β = 0.608), leg BMC (β = 0.429), and pelvis BMC (β = 0.550). Several estimates became smaller or less precise when body mass, projected bone area, or allometric scaling was considered. Pelvis BMC was conditionally associated with estimated leg press 1-RM after adjustment for age, height, and lower body lean mass (β = 0.501; 18 test BH q = 0.001). This association, however, cannot distinguish the influence of skeletal size, body proportions, training history, or other unmeasured factors.

Conclusions

In resistance-trained males, regional DXA lean mass and bone measures appear to form a phenotype that is strongly influenced by body size. Associations from models adjusted for age and height should therefore be interpreted alongside the size conditioned analyzes. The association between pelvis BMC and estimated leg press 1-RM is best viewed as an exploratory conditional finding within this broader phenotype, rather than evidence of a distinct skeletal contribution to strength.

records.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

records.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Engberg Treu Lassen, L, Kersting, UG, and Pessoto Hirata, R. Comparison of functional and traditional strength and power training on U19 soccer players during off-season in Norway: A randomized controlled trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Functional training emphasizes multiplanar, soccer-specific movement patterns requiring body control, whereas traditional resistance training focuses on maximal force production through stable, bilateral lifts. Although both approaches are common in soccer physical preparation, their relative effects on soccer-specific performance remain uncertain. This study compared the effects of functional vs. traditional strength training on performance outcomes during the offseason in U19 male players. Thirty-three Norwegian players were randomly allocated to a functional training group (FTG, n = 11), a traditional training group (TTG, n = 11), or a control group (CG, n = 11) using stratified, concealed allocation. During the first 4 weeks, all groups completed 2 weekly soccer sessions; FTG and TTG additionally completed 2 supervised 70-minute strength sessions per week. In the final 4 weeks, FTG and TTG continued the twice-weekly strength training, whereas CG ceased organized training. Functional training group performed unilateral, multiplanar free-weight exercises, while TTG performed bilateral, uniplanar machine-based exercises. The primary outcome was technical soccer performance, with mobility, dynamic balance, sprint speed, change of direction, and vertical jump as secondary outcomes. Both FTG and TTG improved Loughborough Soccer Shooting Test (LSST) performance compared with CG (FTG: -0.43 seconds, p = 0.003, d = 1.62; TTG: -0.50 seconds, p < 0.001, d = 1.88). Traditional training group also increased body mass compared with the CG (2.20 kg, p = 0.002, d = 1.65). Functional and traditional strength training produced comparable improvements in LSST time. These findings highlight training dose response and support individualized off-season programs integrating physical preparation with sport-specific demands.

records.title: Impact of different protein sources on acute muscle protein synthesis following resistance training: a systematic review with standard and dose-response network meta-analyses.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Impact of different protein sources on acute muscle protein synthesis following resistance training: a systematic review with standard and dose-response network meta-analyses.
content.abstract:
Background

The combination of protein intake and resistance training (RT) plays a pivotal role in stimulating muscle protein synthesis (MPS), yet the impact of different protein sources remains an area of active investigation. Therefore, a systematic review incorporating standard and dose‒response network meta-analyses was performed.

Methods

Systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, EBSCOhost (including MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL), and Scopus. Eligible studies included healthy adults (≥18 years) who were undergoing acute resistance exercise followed by a single protein bolus (any type or dose, except blends or enriched with anabolic agents). Muscle biopsies were required before and after RT/protein intake without additional food in between. Trials measuring hourly MPS rates via tracer techniques were included (n = 51).

Results

In the standard network meta-analysis (NMA), native whey (P-score = 0.81, MD = 0.05% [0.00; 0.10]), pea protein (0.77, MD = 0.05% [-0.02; 0.11]), whole egg protein (0.72, MD = 0.04% [-0.01; 0.09]), mycoprotein (0.66, MD = 0.03% [-0.02; 0.08]), and whey protein (0.58, MD = 0.02% [0.01; 0.04]) ranked highest for estimated efficacy in stimulating post-RT hourly MPS (in descending order) (only whey protein showed a statistically significant effect) with low to moderate certainty of evidence. Dose‒response NMA revealed that certain animal- (native whey and whole egg protein) and plant- (pea and mycoprotein) based protein sources to show the highest predicted MPS responses with doses of 18-25 g.

Conclusions

Animal- (native whey, whey, whole egg) and plant-based (pea, mycoprotein) proteins ranked similarly for estimated acute MPS stimulation when combined with RT; however, only whey protein showed a statistically significant effect, and protein sources represented by few studies should be interpreted with caution.

records.title: Effects of Prolonged Combined Aerobic and Strength Training on Movement Velocities During a Strength Loading Bout: Targeting Same Versus Separate Muscle Groups.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of Prolonged Combined Aerobic and Strength Training on Movement Velocities During a Strength Loading Bout: Targeting Same Versus Separate Muscle Groups.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Feuerbacher, JF, Jacobs, MW, Dragutinovic, B, Rehbein, P, and Schumann, M. Effects of prolonged combined aerobic and strength training on movement velocities during a strength loading bout: targeting same versus separate muscle groups. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Combined aerobic and strength training may impair explosive strength performance, especially when targeting the same muscle groups. This study aimed to assess the effects of prolonged combined aerobic and strength training on movement velocities and velocity loss during a strength loading bout when the aerobic and strength training target the same vs. separate muscle groups. Thirty-two men participated in a 12-week intervention, divided into 3 groups: (a) LHLS (lower-body high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and strength training), (b) LHUS (lower-body HIIT and upper-body strength training), and (c) LSUS (lower- and upper-body strength training). Changes in the area under the mean propulsive velocity (MPV) and velocity-loss curves during strength loadings were analyzed pre- and postintervention. Squat performance was compared between LHLS and LSUS, while bench press performance was compared between LHUS and LSUS. The level of significance was set at ρ ≤ 0.05. During bench press loading, no statistically significant main effects for group ( p = 0.225), for timepoint ( p = 0.170), nor group × timepoint ( p = 0.943) were observed for MPV. In squat loading, a statistically significant main effect for timepoint was found ( p = 0.020), with a decrease in MPV for LHLS postintervention ( p = 0.006). The interaction between group and timepoint was not statistically significant ( p = 0.083). No statistically significant main effects for group ( p = 0.110, p = 0.076), for timepoint ( p = 0.590, p = 0.244), nor group × timepoint ( p = 0.626, p = 0.239) were observed for velocity loss in either bench press or squat loading. These findings suggest that explosive strength performance may be more susceptible to interference when aerobic and strength training target the same, rather than different, muscle groups.

records.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
content.abstract:
Background

High-protein diets have consistently been associated with favorable changes in body composition in both sedentary and exercise-trained populations. Despite abundant evidence supporting protein intakes above the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for active individuals, the effects of deliberate protein overfeeding, particularly in those already consuming adequate protein, remain incompletely characterized. The primary purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition in exercise-trained men and women. The secondary purpose was to determine whether body composition adaptations differed by FTO rs9939609 genotype.

Methods

Fifty-six exercise-trained men and women (age: 22.40 ± 5.78 years; body mass: 75.47 ± 14.98 kg; BMI: 24.52 ± 3.50 kg/m2; resistance training: 5.12 ± 3.35 h/week) were enrolled in a 4-week dietary intervention. Participants were instructed to increase their daily protein intake by approximately 20% above baseline while maintaining habitual training. Body composition was assessed pre- and post-intervention using a multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance device (InBody® 270). Dietary intake was self-monitored via MyFitnessPal®. Thirty-five participants completed both pre- and post-testing assessments and constituted the primary analysis. Linear regression models adjusted for baseline values indicated that FTO genotype was not a significant predictor of body composition changes (p > 0.05).

Results

Protein intake trended toward a significant increase over the 4-week period (pre: 146 ± 66 g/day vs. post: 164 ± 79 g/day; p = 0.053), representing an approximate 12% increase. Total energy intake, carbohydrate, and fat intake did not significantly change. Lean body mass increased significantly (pre: 59.95 ± 14.14 kg vs. post: 60.62 ± 14.42 kg; p = 0.005; Cohen's d = 0.31) and total body water increased significantly (pre: 43.85 ± 10.35 L vs. post: 44.34 ± 10.55 L; p = 0.005). Fat mass (p = 0.424), body fat percentage (p = 0.149), and total body mass (p = 0.09) did not significantly change.

Conclusions

A 4-week modest protein overfeeding protocol in exercise-trained men and women was associated with a significant increase in lean body mass and total body water without concomitant increases in fat mass. These adaptations were not modified by FTO rs9939609 genotype. These findings support the contention that higher protein intakes do not promote fat accretion and may facilitate improvements in body composition in trained individuals.

records.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Sebastian-Rico, JM, Muñoz-Fernández, MJ, Martínez-Aranda, LM, Calvo-Lluch, Á, and Ortega-Becerra, M. Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training in women soccer players and its relationship with quality of life and pelvic floor muscle strength: a randomized controlled pilot study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of a 6-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program on muscle strength, function, and the prevalence of related dysfunctions in professional female soccer players using a randomized controlled pilot study design. Twenty nulliparous professional soccer players from the Spanish professional league (2024-2025 season) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 8). Assessments included anthropometric data, validated questionnaires (International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form and Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), clinical interviews, and physical examination using the PERFECT method and manometry. The intervention consisted of a 6-week supervised PFMT program (4 sessions/week, 30 minutes each) progressed through 4 phases: education, proprioception, strengthening, and functional integration. Results showed significant group × time interactions for pelvic floor self-efficacy (Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), with scores in the PFMT group increasing by 48.8 and 59.6% (p < 0.05), representing large between-group effect sizes (d = 0.91-1.26). Pelvic floor muscle performance increased by 122.4% in the intervention group (d = 1.25), whereas no meaningful changes were observed in the control group. No adverse events were reported. In conclusion, a 6-week supervised PFMT program is an effective and safe intervention for professional female soccer players, significantly improving muscle function and self-efficacy. These findings support the integration of PFMT for both therapeutic and preventive purposes in elite, high-impact sports environments.

records.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
content.abstract:
Background

High protein intake is common among resistance-trained athletes, but its association with renal biomarkers across different exercise modalities remains uncertain. This study investigated whether consuming a high-protein diet (3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹) during 16 weeks of resistance training (RT) or concurrent training (CT) affects renal biomarkers and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in resistance-trained men.

Methods

Forty-eight resistance-trained men (26 ± 6 years; BMI 25.6 ± 2.9 kg·m⁻²) were randomized to 16 weeks of RT or CT (4 sessions·wk⁻¹) while consuming either 1.6 or 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ of protein in a 2 × 2 factorial design. Forty-four participants with complete pre- and post-intervention data were analyzed. Fasting blood samples were assessed for blood urea nitrogen (BUN), BUN/creatinine ratio, cystatin C, and eGFR calculated using the CKD-EPI creatinine (2021), cystatin C (2012), and creatinine-cystatin C (2021) equations. Within-group changes were evaluated using paired t-tests, and factorial effects were assessed using linear mixed-effects models (Time × Training × Protein).

Results

No statistically significant Time × Protein or Time × Training × Protein interactions were detected for any renal biomarker or eGFR estimate (all p ≥ 0.182). No significant within-group changes occurred in the 1.6 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups (all p > 0.05). In both 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups, BUN and cystatin C increased (all p ≤ 0.017), while eGFR estimates decreased (all p ≤ 0.009). The BUN/creatinine ratio remained unchanged (p ≥ 0.614). However, these within-group findings were descriptive because the corresponding interaction effects were not statistically significant.

Conclusions

In resistance-trained men, 16 weeks of high protein intake did not produce statistically detectable differences in renal biomarker or eGFR changes compared with moderate protein intake, irrespective of training modality. Although modest increases in BUN and cystatin C and small decreases in eGFR estimates were observed within the high-protein groups, these findings were not supported by significant factorial interactions. The limited sample size precludes excluding clinically meaningful differences, warranting further investigation in larger studies.

records.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

records.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
content.abstract: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) has developed an official position on diets for body weight reduction. This critical analysis of the literature is intended to provide a scientific foundation for practitioners, coaches, and trainees regarding the effects of the major diet types in adults who are generally healthy, physically active, and/or athletic, while drawing from clinical research in those with overweight/obesity, when relevant. This position stand does not address acute dehydration-based weight cutting, pharmacotherapy (i.e. GLP-1RAs), or bariatric surgery. The following 15 points constitute the Position Statement of the Society; the Research Committee has approved them. 1) Diets for body weight reduction can be broadly categorized by the magnitude of the energy deficit, linearity of the deficit, and macronutrient composition. These factors need to be tailored to individual preferences, tolerances, and goals.2) Very-low-energy diets (<800 kcal/day) and low-energy diets (800-1200  kcal/day) produce greater short-term weight loss but lack long-term advantages over less aggressive energy restrictions, such as calorie-controlled diets. These aggressive diets may increase lean mass loss, although adequate protein intake and resistance training may mitigate this risk. Caution is warranted about insufficiencies in vitamins, minerals, fiber, and other nutrients.3) The evidence at-large shows a lack of differential effects between intermittent fasting variants (alternate-day fasting, time-restricted eating, and twice-weekly fasting) and continuous energy restriction on anthropometric outcomes, although macronutrient quality plays an independent role in optimizing body composition and metabolic health.4) Intra-day meal frequency (as opposed to total daily nutrition) does not tend to crucially influence body weight and body fat reduction. Meal frequency may be individualized flexibly; no lower or upper limits can universally be prescribed to optimize outcomes. However, in physically active and athletic populations, distributing protein across at least three protein-rich meals (or eating occasions) per day may optimize lean mass retention and performance during sustained energy deficits.5) Resistance training and sufficient protein intake are indispensable mitigators of lean mass loss in a sustained caloric deficit, regardless of the diet type or variant. Total daily protein is of primary importance; specific distribution of the constituent doses is a secondary concern.6) For the general population, a daily protein intake of 1.2-1.6 g/kg BW is appropriate for supporting total body weight and fat loss, physical activity, and imparting benefits to musculoskeletal and cardiometabolic health.7) Daily protein intakes ranging 1.6-2.2 g/kg BW combined with resistance training may optimize muscle anabolism, while higher intakes of 1.9-3.2 g/kg BW can maximize lean mass retention in lean, resistance-trained individuals sustaining hypocaloric conditions.8) The dietary carbohydrate‒fat proportion can be individualized to personal preference for the goal of weight loss, since the range of ketogenic to low-fat diets performs similarly.9) Ketogenic diets are effective at bodyweight and body fat reduction, but they also tend to decrease fat-free mass to a greater degree than higher-carbohydrate comparators, particularly in shorter trials where glycogen and total body water shifts can influence estimates.10) Adaptations to weight loss can be physical, physiological, and/or behavioral, and converge toward reducing energy expenditure to fulfill the body's drive toward neutralizing disruptions to homeostasis imposed by the caloric deficit.11) Adaptive thermogenesis is a reduction in resting energy expenditure beyond that predicted by changes in body composition. It can occur in response to hypocaloric conditions and weight loss, but it is not an inevitable response, and it may attenuate substantially upon attainment of weight stability.12) Metabolic adaptations that reduce energy expenditure, including adaptive thermogenesis, and impair gut microbial diversity, can often be attenuated by strategic dietary and exercise programming that foster nutrient-absorption and partitioning, and metabolic flexibility.13) A multitude of tactics can be implemented to manage and overcome plateaus. However, plateaus are also opportunities/cues to practice maintaining progress made thus far (the ultimate goal is the maintenance of a plateau).14) Guidance from an interdisciplinary team of health professionals while maintaining social support is recommended for successful weight management.15) Learning how to prepare home-cooked meals (and plan meals ahead of time through the day) puts dieters in control of their nutritional fate - and in a better position to succeed in managing their body weight and body composition.

records.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
content.abstract:
Purpose

The primary purpose of this study was to investigate whether isometric resistance training (RT) leads to reticulospinal tract (RST) adaptations.

Methods

A "RT group" of 30 healthy adults completed 4 weeks (15 sessions) of volume-matched unilateral elbow flexion RT involving high (32 repetitions/session at 70% maximal voluntary torque [MVT]) or low (64 repetitions/session at 35%MVT) loads. An additional 15 participants served as controls (CON group). Pre- and post-test MVT, RST properties (RST gain ratio derived from the StartReact assessment; startling auditory stimulus-conditioned/control motor evoked potential [MEP] ratio; and startling stimulus-conditioned/control cervicomedullary MEP [CMEP] ratio), CST excitability and intracortical inhibition properties (in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation) were assessed.

Results

MVT increased more in the RT group (+12.8%; n = 30) vs. CON group (-4.3%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), p = 0.001). However, changes in RST properties assessed using a series of indirect measures did not differ between the RT group (-1.4% to 6.6%; n = 30) and CON group (-4.5% to 10.5%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), 0.352 ≤ p ≤ 0.834).

Conclusions

RST adaptations within a sample of healthy young men and women, assessed using various indirect measurement approaches, did not occur following only 4 weeks of isometric elbow flexion RT. These findings add to the currently limited scientific evidence from short-term human RT intervention studies available to inform the use of RT for healthy individuals or patients primarily targeting the development of RST function.

records.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
content.abstract:
Purpose

The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females.

Methods

Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness.

Results

Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p<0.05), and RTL had more fat-free mass than SL and SB (RTL = 48.31±5.81 kg; SL = 38.08±6.59 kg; SB = 40.37±6.05 kg; both p<0.05). There were no differences between RTL and RTB in bone mineral density, muscle quality, or physical performance. RTL outperformed SL and SB on vertical jump (both p<0.05) while RTB outperformed SL and SB on broad jump. RTL had lower fasting blood glucose than RTB (88.92±12.09 mg/dL and 103.17 ± 10.21 mg/dL, respectively; p=0.008), and lower postprandial blood glucose than all groups (RTL = 103.83±19.82 mg/dL; RTB = 137.58±21.54 mg/dL; SL = 148.50±44.60 mg/dL; SB = 139.25±14.49 mg/dL; all p<0.05).

Conclusions

The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

records.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Yan, X, Zuo, Z, Nitsche, MA, Zhang, X, and Qi, F. Multiple sessions of transcranial direct current stimulation combined with squat training improve lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to investigate the effects of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with Squat training (ST) on lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. Sixty men (age: 21.6 ± 2.1 years, height: 177.5 ± 5.3 cm, body mass: 73.1 ± 7.4 kg) were randomly assigned to 4 groups (tDCS + ST group, sham tDCS + ST group, tDCS + rest group, sham tDCS + rest group). The 6-week intervention program was implemented with biweekly sessions, totaling 12 treatment sessions, each separated by a minimum 48-hour interval.
